blueprint.speaker: Ines Halvorsen, a literary translator from Norwegian into English who writes a long-form blog called The Margin
blueprint.audience: readers of literary fiction, book reviewers, prize administrators and publishers, plus fellow translators
blueprint.exigence: The fictional Ambervale Prize announced its shortlist in a press release that named authors and publishers but no translators, though the writer translated one of the shortlisted novels
blueprint.purpose: To persuade readers and the publishing world that translators are co-authors of the English text and should be named on covers, in press releases and in reviews
blueprint.context: A personal blog post written in the week after the shortlist announcement, drawing on the writer's own experience translating a novel by the fictional Norwegian novelist Sigrun Aalvik
blueprint.claim: Because every English sentence in a translated novel is the translator's decision, translators are authors of the books readers actually read, and their invisibility is a chosen convention that should be reversed by naming them
blueprint.line_of_reasoning: Opens with the prize anecdote showing the omission (P1); dismantles the plumbing model of translation and shows through the 'weather' example that translation is a chain of authorial choices (P2); scales that example up with a count of decisions to argue the English sentences are the translator's (P3); concedes the author owns story and characters but rebuts through the carpenter analogy (P4); asks why invisibility persists and enumerates three causes that form a circle (P5); shifts to a modest proposal and direct address to prize runners, reviewers and readers (P6)
evidence_types: specific textual example from a translation
rough self-reported count presented as a statistic

devices.function: Establishes the exigence and the writer's firsthand stake through the prize press release
The translator's name is smaller than the note about paper stock, exposing the absurd priority of credit
The plumbing analogy states the popular view so it can be rejected
Short sentences after long ones deliver the verdict bluntly
Redefines a sentence as a set of choices rather than a container of meaning
The 'went out into the weather' example shows one authorial choice forced on the translator
The rough count of forty decisions a page scales the single example into a book-wide claim
Matching fronted clauses claim authorship of both praise and blame
Admired versus clumsy sentences both end in 'I wrote'
Grants the author's ownership of story and characters, then rebuts with the carpenter analogy
'There is something to this' concedes minimally before the turn
Carpenter and architect analogy reframes the translator's contribution as creditable craft
Pivots from establishing authorship to diagnosing why it goes uncredited
Three 'partly' causes organize the diagnosis
Shows the three causes forming a self-reinforcing circle
The colon announces the circular explanation that the two following clauses enact
Limits the proposal to avoid seeming to displace the author
Assigns concrete actions to prize runners, reviewers and readers
Repeated 'If you...' clauses make the call to action feel orderly and modest
Reminds readers they have already loved a translator's work without knowing it

blueprint.counterargument: The story, characters and architecture of a novel belong to the original author, so the translator is at most a skilled craftsperson executing someone else's design (sentences 16-18); rebutted by the carpenter analogy in sentences 19-20

provenance.venue_alias: The Margin (a personal blog on translation)
provenance.note: Entirely fictional writer, prize, novelist and figures.

g-lr11.title: Who Wrote the English Sentences
paragraphs: Last Tuesday the Ambervale Prize announced its shortlist, and the press release named six novels, six authors, and six publishers, but not one translator.
Four of those six books were written in languages the jury does not read.
I know this because I translated one of them.
My name appears on page four of the paperback, in a typeface smaller than the one used to describe the paper stock.
Readers sometimes imagine translation as a kind of plumbing: the words flow in one end of the pipe in Norwegian and come out the other end in English, and the translator merely checks for leaks.
The image is comforting, and it is wrong.
A sentence in one language is not a container with a fixed amount of meaning inside it; it is a set of choices that a second language cannot reproduce but can only answer.
When the Norwegian novelist Sigrun Aalvik wrote that her heroine "went out into the weather," she used a verb that in her dialect also means to quarrel.
English has no such verb.
I had to decide whether the woman walked into a storm or into an argument, and whichever I chose, the English reader would believe the author had chosen it.
Consider the scale of the problem.

Aalvik's novel runs to roughly ninety thousand words, and I made, by my own rough count, something near forty decisions a page that no dictionary could make for me: where to break a sentence, which of three possible synonyms carried the right chill, whether a joke survived or had to be replaced with a different joke.
Multiply that by three hundred pages and you arrive at an English book that shares a plot and a spirit with the Norwegian one but shares none of its sentences.
Every sentence the English reader admires, I wrote.
Every sentence the reader finds clumsy, I also wrote.

I can hear the objection, because I have made it myself at dinner parties: the story, the characters, the architecture of the book belong to Aalvik, and the translator is at most a skilled carpenter working from her drawings.
There is something to this.
I did not invent the heroine, and I would not want credit for her.
But a carpenter who selects every board, every joint, and every finish, and whose work the client lives inside for years, is not usually left off the plaque.
Architecture is credited; so is the building.
Why, then, does the convention of the invisible translator persist?
Partly because publishers fear that a second name on the cover warns the buyer that the book is foreign, and foreign, in the sales meeting, means difficult.
Partly because reviewers, who seldom read the original, find it easier to praise "the author's luminous prose" than to admit they are praising prose whose author they cannot identify.
And partly, I confess, because translators themselves have cultivated a monkish modesty, as though visibility were a kind of vanity.
The effect is circular: because we are unnamed, we seem unimportant, and because we seem unimportant, nobody thinks to name us.
I am not asking for the author's name to be removed, or shrunk, or shared with mine in some awkward hyphenated compound.
I am asking for a line of type on the front of the book, the same size as the blurb from a novelist nobody has heard of, that says who wrote the English sentences.
If you run a prize, name the translator in the press release.
If you review books, say which words you are actually quoting.
And if you are a reader who has ever loved a novel written in a language you do not speak, you have already loved a translator's work; you simply were not told whom to thank.

items.stem: In paragraph 4, the writer's admission of having made the objection "myself at dinner parties" most likely appeals to the audience by

options.text: signaling that the writer has largely abandoned the claim to authorship, so that readers who revere the original novelist will not feel threatened by the rest of the post
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer concedes only story and characters and immediately rebuts with the carpenter analogy; the writer does not abandon the authorship claim.

options.text: suggesting that readers who hold the objection are in reasonable company, so that the writer's rebuttal reads as a conclusion the writer reached rather than a defense of the writer's own interests
options.label: correct
options.why: By owning the objection and granting 'There is something to this,' the writer disarms readers who share it and makes the carpenter rebuttal seem considered rather than self-serving.

options.text: showing that the objection is trivial enough to be raised casually over dinner, so that readers will dismiss outright the view that the story belongs to the novelist
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: She treats the objection seriously ('There is something to this,' 'I would not want credit for her'); the dinner-party detail shows familiarity, not triviality.

options.text: establishing that the writer's audience consists chiefly of literary insiders who attend such gatherings, so that the argument can rely on their specialized knowledge of publishing customs and the conventions of prize juries
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Nothing in the passage limits the audience to insiders; the final paragraph addresses prize runners, reviewers and ordinary readers.

items.stem: The sentence "Four of those six books were written in languages the jury does not read" (paragraph 1) primarily functions as

options.text: evidence that the prize's judgment of most of its shortlist depended on translators' work, which makes the omission of their names consequential rather than clerical
options.label: correct
options.why: The detail shows the jury could only read those four books through translation, sharpening the point that the press release omitted the people responsible for what the jury read.

options.text: a concession that the prize rightly focused on authors, since the jury could only assess the stories rather than the prose of most entries
options.label: reversal
options.why: The sentence intensifies the criticism of the press release; it does not grant that the focus on authors was correct.

options.text: a claim that the jury lacked the linguistic qualifications to evaluate foreign novels fairly, which the rest of the paragraph proceeds to support
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The writer never argues the jury was unqualified; the sentence is a factual detail supporting the omission point, not a thesis about the jury's competence.

options.text: evidence that translated novels now outnumber English-language novels on literary shortlists across the industry, a trend which explains the writer's interest in this particular prize
options.label: too_broad
options.why: One shortlist with four of six translated books is not offered as a trend across shortlists; the passage makes no such generalization.

items.stem: The example of the heroine who "went out into the weather" (paragraph 2) most directly supports which of the following claims made in the passage?

options.text: Publishers fear that a second name on the cover will mark a book as foreign and therefore difficult for buyers in the sales meeting
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: That claim concerns marketing in paragraph 5; the weather example is about linguistic choice, not sales fears.

options.text: A sentence is a set of choices that a second language cannot reproduce but can only answer, and the translator's answer is taken as the author's
options.label: correct
options.why: The verb with a double meaning has no English equivalent, forcing the translator to choose, and 'the English reader would believe the author had chosen it' directly illustrates the claim in the preceding sentence.

options.text: Translators have cultivated a monkish modesty that treats visibility as a form of vanity and keeps their names off covers and out of press releases
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: The modesty claim appears in paragraph 5 as a cause of invisibility; the example does not touch translators' attitudes toward credit.

options.text: The story, the characters, and the architecture of a novel belong to the original novelist rather than to the person who translates it
options.label: partially_right
options.why: The example does involve Aalvik's heroine, but it is used to show the translator's authorship of the sentence, not the novelist's ownership of story.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the method of development in paragraph 5 and the reason the writer uses it?

options.text: Enumeration of three causes that together form a self-reinforcing loop, used to show that invisibility is a maintained convention rather than a natural fact
options.label: correct
options.why: The question in the first sentence is answered by three 'partly because' causes and then the colon sentence shows the causes feeding one another, which supports the claim that the convention persists by choice and habit.

options.text: Classification of translators into types according to how much modesty they display, used to show which translators deserve to be named on covers
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Translators are not sorted into types; modesty is mentioned once as a cause, and the writer argues all translators should be named.

options.text: Comparison and contrast between publishers and reviewers, used to show that the two groups have opposite reasons for ignoring translators and therefore require opposite remedies
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The three groups are presented as contributing to one shared effect, not as contrasting opposites, and no separate remedies are distinguished.

options.text: Narration of the writer's own experiences with publishers, used to show that the writer has personally suffered from each of the practices described
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The paragraph offers general causes, not narrated episodes; the only personal note is 'I confess,' which admits a shared habit.

items.stem: In paragraph 5, the colon in the sentence beginning "The effect is circular" is effective primarily because it

options.text: separates the three causes listed earlier from the writer's confession, so that readers see the writer's own modesty as the decisive reason translators go unnamed
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The confession occurs in the previous sentence; the colon introduces the summary effect, and the three causes are given equal weight.

options.text: announces that an explanation of the word "circular" follows, and the two clauses after it then trace the loop the word names, so form and claim match
options.label: correct
options.why: The colon sets up the explanation, and the paired 'because...because' clauses move from unnamed to unimportant and back to unnamed, enacting the circle.

options.text: introduces a list of further parties who contribute to the convention, so that the explanation extends beyond the three groups named in the paragraph
options.label: unsupported
options.why: No additional parties follow the colon; what follows is a two-step causal loop about translators being unnamed and seeming unimportant.

options.text: creates a pause that softens the accusation against publishers and reviewers, so that the tone of the paragraph becomes more conciliatory before the proposal
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The sentence does not soften anything; it states the self-reinforcing problem bluntly, and the shift to proposal comes in the next paragraph.

items.stem: The details in paragraph 1 suggest that the passage was most immediately prompted by

options.text: a prize announcement that credited authors and publishers while omitting the translators of most of the shortlisted books
options.label: correct
options.why: Sentences 1-3 describe the Ambervale Prize press release naming six novels, authors and publishers but no translator, though four of the six were translated, including one by the writer.

options.text: a publisher's decision to print the writer's name on an inside page rather than on the cover of a recent paperback
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Sentence 4 mentions the small typeface on page four as a supporting illustration of the problem, but the opening event that occasions the post is the shortlist press release, not a single publisher's layout.

options.text: a jury's refusal to consider novels written in languages that its members are unable to read
options.label: reversal
options.why: Sentence 2 says four shortlisted books were written in languages the jury does not read, so the jury did consider them; the complaint is about credit, not exclusion.

options.text: a reviewer's claim that the prose of a translated novel belonged entirely to its original author
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Reviewers who praise 'the author's luminous prose' appear in sentence 23 as one general cause of invisibility, not as the specific event in paragraph 1 that prompted the passage.

items.stem: In the final sentence of the passage, the writer's reminder to readers who have "ever loved a novel written in a language you do not speak" appeals to the audience primarily by

options.text: recasting the demand for credit as a chance for readers to acknowledge a debt they have unknowingly already incurred
options.label: correct
options.why: Sentence 30 tells readers they 'have already loved a translator's work' and 'simply were not told whom to thank,' turning the request into gratitude readers already owe rather than a new burden.

options.text: warning readers that their admiration for foreign novels has been misdirected toward authors who did not deserve it
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The sentence is warm and inclusive, not accusatory; sentence 26 explicitly declines to diminish the author, so the appeal does not suggest authors are undeserving.

options.text: inviting readers to feel superior to reviewers and prize juries who have failed to notice translators
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Nothing in sentence 30 sets readers against reviewers or juries; those groups receive their own instructions in sentences 28-29, and readers are addressed on their own terms.

options.text: suggesting that readers who learn foreign languages will no longer need translators at all
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The passage never proposes that readers learn languages; the appeal depends on readers continuing to rely on translations and simply naming those who make them.

items.stem: Taken together, the instructions in paragraph 6 indicate that the writer imagines an audience that

options.text: is made up of fellow translators who need encouragement to abandon their habitual modesty
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Translators are mentioned in sentence 24 as one cause of the problem, but paragraph 6 addresses prize runners, reviewers and ordinary readers, not translators.

options.text: includes people in several different roles, each able to change one specific practice
options.label: correct
options.why: Sentences 28-30 address in turn those who run prizes, those who review books, and readers, assigning each a concrete action, which signals a mixed audience of readers and industry participants.

options.text: consists mainly of publishers who must be persuaded that foreign books are not difficult to sell
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Publishers' fears appear in sentence 22 as a diagnosis, but paragraph 6 does not address publishers directly; its 'If you' clauses name prizes, reviewers and readers.

options.text: shares the writer's expertise and already agrees that translators deserve to be named
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The patient explanation of the plumbing misconception in paragraph 2 and the final reminder that readers 'were not told whom to thank' assume an audience that has not yet considered the issue.

items.stem: Which of the following best states the central claim of the passage as a whole?

options.text: Because the English sentences of a translated novel are the translator's own decisions, the translator should be named as the person who wrote them
options.label: correct
options.why: Paragraphs 2-3 establish that every English sentence is the translator's choice (sentences 10, 13-15), and paragraph 6 draws the conclusion that a line on the cover should say 'who wrote the English sentences' (sentence 27).

options.text: Because translation changes every sentence of a novel, a translated book is essentially a new work that belongs to the translator rather than the author
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Sentences 18 and 26 explicitly deny this: the writer did not invent the heroine, does not want credit for her, and is not asking for the author's name to be removed or shrunk.

options.text: Because publishers believe that foreign books are difficult to sell, translators will remain invisible until the economics of publishing change
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Publishers' fear is only the first of three causes listed in paragraph 5, and the passage ends with a practical remedy rather than resignation about economics.

options.text: Because translators have cultivated a monkish modesty, they are themselves chiefly responsible for the convention that leaves them unnamed
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Sentence 24 does admit translators' modesty as one cause, but it is one of three 'partly' causes, and the thesis concerns authorship and credit rather than assigning blame to translators.

items.stem: The writer's statement in paragraph 6 that she is "not asking for the author's name to be removed, or shrunk, or shared with mine in some awkward hyphenated compound" primarily serves to

options.text: concede that the original author contributes more to a novel than the translator does and therefore deserves a larger share of the credit
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The sentence limits what is being requested; it does not weigh the relative size of contributions, and paragraph 3 has already claimed full authorship of the English sentences.

options.text: forestall the fear that crediting translators would displace authors, so that the request that follows seems modest and easy to grant
options.label: correct
options.why: Sentence 26 rules out every version of the proposal that might threaten the author's standing before sentence 27 asks only for 'a line of type' the size of a blurb, making the demand hard to refuse.

options.text: acknowledge that publishers' concerns about cover design are legitimate and that translators should accept inside-page credit
options.label: reversal
options.why: Sentence 27 asks for the translator's name 'on the front of the book,' so the writer rejects inside-page credit, which sentence 4 treated with irony.

options.text: introduce a new counterargument about shared authorship that the remaining sentences of the paragraph then refute in detail
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The remaining sentences (27-30) state the proposal and assign actions; they do not refute a counterargument, and the objection about shared credit is dismissed within sentence 26 itself.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the relationship between paragraph 2 and paragraph 3?

options.text: Paragraph 2 presents the popular view of translation, and paragraph 3 offers a competing popular view that the writer also rejects
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Paragraph 3 does not present another popular view; it builds on the writer's own account from paragraph 2 by counting the decisions across a whole novel.

options.text: Paragraph 2 shows a single forced choice in one sentence, and paragraph 3 multiplies that choice across the whole novel to claim its sentences
options.label: correct
options.why: Sentences 8-10 isolate one decision about 'the weather'; sentence 11 says 'Consider the scale,' and sentences 12-15 multiply roughly forty decisions a page by three hundred pages to conclude 'Every sentence... I wrote.'

options.text: Paragraph 2 argues that translation is impossible, and paragraph 3 reverses course to show that most sentences survive translation intact
options.label: reversal
options.why: Sentence 13 says the English book 'shares none of its sentences' with the Norwegian one, so paragraph 3 intensifies rather than reverses the point that sentences are remade.

options.text: Paragraph 2 describes the writer's personal method, and paragraph 3 shifts to statistics gathered from other translators to generalize it
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The count in sentence 12 is the writer's own 'rough count' of her own work on Aalvik's novel; no other translators or outside data appear.

items.stem: The question that opens paragraph 5, "Why, then, does the convention of the invisible translator persist?", contributes to the coherence of the passage primarily by

options.text: treating the translator's authorship as settled by the preceding paragraphs and turning the argument toward the causes of a problem
options.label: correct
options.why: The word 'then' in sentence 21 assumes paragraphs 2-4 have established authorship; the question redirects the passage from proving the claim to diagnosing why credit is withheld, which sentences 22-25 answer.

options.text: reopening the objection from paragraph 4 so that the writer can concede that the convention has some justification
options.label: reversal
options.why: Paragraph 4 ends with the rebuttal 'Architecture is credited; so is the building'; sentence 21 does not revive the objection but asks why a practice already shown to be unjust continues.

options.text: signaling that the writer will now abandon personal experience in favor of a survey of publishing history
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Paragraph 5 still speaks personally ('I confess' in sentence 24) and offers three present-day causes, not a history of publishing.

options.text: introducing the specific remedy that paragraph 6 will later request from prize committees and reviewers
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The question asks for causes, which paragraph 5 supplies; the remedy is introduced only in sentences 26-27 after the diagnosis is complete.

items.stem: The instruction in paragraph 6, "If you run a prize, name the translator in the press release," strengthens the line of reasoning of the passage as a whole chiefly because it

options.text: returns to the specific grievance of the opening paragraph and shows that the general argument yields a concrete fix for it
options.label: correct
options.why: Placeholder

options.text: demonstrates that prize juries, unlike reviewers, are capable of reading the original languages of the novels they judge
options.label: reversal
options.why: Sentence 2 states that the jury does not read the languages of four shortlisted books, so the instruction cannot rest on juries' linguistic ability.

options.text: proves that the three causes enumerated in paragraph 5 can all be eliminated by a single change in prize administration
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Naming translators in press releases addresses prizes only; publishers' fears and reviewers' habits receive separate treatment in sentences 27 and 29.

options.text: shifts the responsibility for translators' invisibility away from the translators who confessed to cultivating modesty
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The instruction assigns a task to prize runners without revisiting the confession in sentence 24; it does not reassign blame, and the passage treats all three causes as jointly operating.

items.stem: In paragraph 1, the detail that the writer's name appears "in a typeface smaller than the one used to describe the paper stock" chiefly establishes a tone that is

options.text: bitterly indignant, preparing the reader for a direct attack on the publisher's negligence
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The sentence states a measurable fact without any angry adjective, and the passage never attacks a particular publisher; paragraph 2 instead turns calmly to explaining a misconception.

options.text: dryly ironic, letting a factual comparison expose how little the translator's contribution is valued
options.label: correct
options.why: Sentence 4 makes no complaint outright; ranking the translator's name below the description of paper exposes the absurd priorities of credit through understated comparison.

options.text: resigned and self-deprecating, suggesting the writer accepts that translators rank below physical materials
options.label: reversal
options.why: The passage goes on to argue forcefully against this ranking (sentences 14-15, 27), so the detail registers a grievance rather than acceptance of it.

options.text: playfully boastful, hinting that the writer's name will soon become as prominent as the author's
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Nothing in sentence 4 predicts future prominence, and sentence 26 explicitly declines any equal or shared billing with the author.

items.stem: In paragraph 4, the sentence beginning "But a carpenter who selects every board, every joint, and every finish, and whose work the client lives inside for years" is structured so as to

options.text: accumulate the carpenter's contributions in subordinate clauses before the brief main clause, so the modest conclusion seems earned
options.label: correct
options.why: Sentence 19 delays its main verb while two relative clauses pile up the carpenter's choices and the client's long residence; the short ending 'is not usually left off the plaque' then lands as an understated, well-supported verdict.

options.text: balance two equal independent clauses so that the carpenter's labor and the architect's design receive matching emphasis
options.label: convention_error
options.why: The sentence has a single main clause with subordinate modifiers; the balanced two-clause structure appears instead in sentence 20, 'Architecture is credited; so is the building.'

options.text: place the main claim first and then qualify it with a list of exceptions in which carpenters do go uncredited
options.label: reversal
options.why: The main claim comes last, not first, and the listed items are the carpenter's contributions supporting credit, not exceptions that withhold it.

options.text: interrupt the argument with a digression about building so that the reader forgets the objection raised earlier in the paragraph
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The carpenter extends the objection's own image from sentence 16 ('a skilled carpenter working from her drawings') in order to answer it, so the structure engages rather than evades the objection.

blueprint.speaker: Delia Hartsook, a columnist for a fictional regional quarterly and a former volunteer firefighter with the Marrow Creek Volunteer Fire Company in fictional Brannock County
blueprint.audience: Readers of a rural regional magazine, especially county commissioners and board members who control fire-service budgets
blueprint.exigence: The publication of a new book, Siren on the Ridge by fictional author Conrad Weil, which argues that the volunteer fire model is obsolete and should be replaced with paid crews
blueprint.purpose: To praise the book's reporting while rejecting its diagnosis, and to persuade county officials that volunteer departments are being starved by unfunded burdens that modest public funding can relieve
blueprint.context: Rural counties facing shrinking, aging volunteer rosters, rising state training requirements, and equipment costs covered by fundraising
blueprint.claim: Volunteer fire service is not obsolete; it is failing because it has been loaded with fundraising and training burdens it was never designed to carry, and those burdens can be lifted by county funding
blueprint.line_of_reasoning: Opens with firsthand anecdote establishing credibility and stakes (P1); credits the book's reporting and grim numbers (P2); concedes the old pattern is gone but rebuts the diagnosis of obsolescence by identifying training and fundraising burdens (P3); uses an analogy to expose the absurdity of self-funded equipment and poses the question the book never asks (P4); answers that question with the Tillery County counterexample (P5); delivers the verdict on the book and a direct appeal to county boards (P6)

devices.function: Opens with the writer's own experience of the pager to establish credibility and the human stakes
Eleven years of service and firsthand knowledge of training hours give the writer authority to judge the book
Weil's grim numbers establish the problem; Tillery's numbers support the writer's remedy
Colons introduce the grim figures and the unasked question with emphasis
Grants that the old pattern is gone, then rejects 'obsolete' as the wrong diagnosis
Lists of fundraising events and roles pile up to show the burden on volunteers
'We did not lose... We lost...' contrasts apathy with overburden
Parallel openings sharpen the corrected diagnosis
Lifeguard and lemonade stand expose the absurdity of self-funded equipment
Poses the question the book fails to ask, setting up paragraph 5
Moves from critical to hopeful as evidence of a remedy is introduced
Two short sentences after longer ones deliver the point with force
'Reaches for the obituary' and 'being starved' contrast premature death-notice with preventable neglect
Speaks directly to county board members to urge action
'Who else would come' frames the essay and closes it

blueprint.counterargument: Weil's view that the volunteer model is obsolete because workers no longer live and work near the station, so counties should hire paid crews; the writer grants the changed work pattern but argues the real cause is unfunded burdens, as the Tillery County levy shows
blueprint.theme: volunteer fire departments in rural counties

provenance.note: Original review essay of a fictional book, Siren on the Ridge by fictional author Conrad Weil. All names, places and figures are invented.

g-lr23.title: Who Else Will Come: On Conrad Weil's Siren on the Ridge
paragraphs: The pager goes off at ten past two in the morning, and for eleven years my first thought was never about the fire but about who else would come.
In Brannock County, where I served with the Marrow Creek Volunteer Fire Company until my knees retired me, a structure fire draws whoever is awake, sober, and within fifteen miles.
Some nights that is nine people; some nights it is three.

Conrad Weil's new book, Siren on the Ridge, is the first account I have read that understands this arithmetic, and it deserves a wide readership among the county commissioners who will decide, over the next decade, whether rural counties keep a volunteer fire service at all.
Weil's reporting is the book's great strength.
He spent two years riding with departments in six counties across three states, and he lets the volunteers speak in their own flat, unsentimental voices.
The numbers he gathers are grim: at one station the average age of a responder rose from thirty-four to fifty-seven in twenty years, and the roster shrank from twenty-two names to nine.
He describes a chief who answers calls alone because there is no one else, and a township that dissolved its company and now waits forty minutes for an engine from the next county.
These are not isolated anecdotes; they are the shape of the thing.
Where the book falters is in its diagnosis.

Weil concludes that the volunteer model is simply obsolete, a relic of a time when men worked within walking distance of the station and could leave the mill when the whistle blew, and he argues that counties should accept the inevitable and hire paid crews.
I grant that the old pattern is gone; nobody leaves a shift at a distribution warehouse forty miles away to answer a brush fire.
But obsolete is the wrong word for a system that has been quietly loaded with burdens it was never designed to carry.
The state now requires one hundred eighty hours of certified training before a recruit may enter a burning building, up from forty when I joined.

The company must also buy its own equipment, which means that the same nine people who fight the fires also run the fish fry, the raffle, the mailer, and the pancake breakfast that pays for the air packs.
We did not lose volunteers because people stopped caring about their neighbors.
We lost them because we asked each one to be a firefighter, a fundraiser, a mechanic, and a grant writer, and then wondered why only retirees had the hours.
Asking a fire company to sell raffle tickets for its own breathing apparatus is like asking a lifeguard to run a lemonade stand to pay for the pool.
The absurdity would be obvious anywhere else.

Yet Weil treats the fundraising burden as a charming folkway rather than the structural failure it is, and so he never asks the question that matters: what happens to the roster when the county, not the fish fry, buys the truck?
We have some evidence, and it is more hopeful than Weil allows.

Tillery County, two hours north of us, passed a modest fire levy six years ago, roughly the price of a tank of gas per household per year, and used it to cover equipment and to reimburse recruits for their training hours.
Its volunteer roster has grown by a third since, and the average age of a new recruit is twenty-nine.
The people were there all along.
They had simply been priced out of serving.
So read Siren on the Ridge for its portraits, which are honest and often moving, and for its warning, which is overdue.
But read it skeptically when it reaches for the obituary.
Volunteer fire service is not dying of old age; it is being starved, and starvation, unlike age, has a remedy.
If you sit on a county board, the remedy is in your budget.
The pager will go off tonight somewhere in your district, and the only question that matters is who else will come.

items.stem: Which of the following sentences best states the central claim of the passage?

options.text: "Its volunteer roster has grown by a third since, and the average age of a new recruit is twenty-nine."
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: This line is evidence from the Tillery County example in paragraph 5 supporting the claim; it reports a result rather than stating the argument.

options.text: "These are not isolated anecdotes; they are the shape of the thing."
options.label: partially_right
options.why: This line in paragraph 2 endorses Weil's evidence that decline is real, which the writer accepts, but it does not express her distinctive claim about the cause of that decline or the remedy.

options.text: "Weil's reporting is the book's great strength."
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: This opening line of paragraph 2 praises one feature of the book; it is a subordinate judgment that the writer goes on to qualify, not the thesis of the review.

options.text: "But obsolete is the wrong word for a system that has been quietly loaded with burdens it was never designed to carry."
options.label: correct
options.why: This line in paragraph 3 states the writer's core disagreement with Weil and the alternative diagnosis that paragraphs 3 through 6 develop: the system is overburdened, not obsolete.

items.stem: Paragraph 1 prepares the reader for the structure of the argument that follows primarily by

options.text: announcing that the review will endorse the book's recommendations for county commissioners without reservation and adopt its proposal for paid crews
options.label: reversal
options.why: Paragraph 1 recommends the book, but paragraph 3 rejects Weil's recommendation to hire paid crews and paragraph 6 urges skepticism.

options.text: pairing the writer's firsthand knowledge with the stakes for county officials, setting up a review that tests the book against experience
options.label: correct
options.why: The opening of paragraph 1 establishes the writer's experience of understaffed calls, and its last sentence names both the book and the commissioners who must decide; the rest of the essay measures Weil's diagnosis against what the writer knows.

options.text: introducing the fire levy adopted in Tillery County as the standard by which the book will be judged
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: The levy does not appear until paragraph 5; paragraph 1 mentions no remedy of any kind.

options.text: outlining a chronological history of the writer's eleven years with the Marrow Creek company that the later paragraphs will continue year by year
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The paragraph gives a single scene and a credential, and no later paragraph narrates the writer's career in sequence.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the relationship between paragraph 3 and paragraph 4?

options.text: Paragraph 4 restates the burden described in paragraph 3 as an analogy and uses it to expose a question the book never asks
options.label: correct
options.why: Paragraph 4 renders paragraph 3's burden of buying the company's own equipment as the lifeguard analogy, then uses that absurdity to pose the question Weil fails to ask.

options.text: Paragraph 4 concedes that Weil's diagnosis in paragraph 3 is correct before offering an alternative remedy drawn from the writer's own years of service
options.label: reversal
options.why: Paragraph 4 criticizes Weil for treating the burden as 'a charming folkway'; it sharpens the disagreement rather than conceding, and it offers no remedy from the writer's service.

options.text: Paragraph 4 narrows the discussion from fundraising to the state training requirement introduced in paragraph 3, treating training hours as the chief burden
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Training is mentioned in paragraph 3, but paragraph 4 concerns fundraising for equipment, not training hours.

options.text: Paragraph 4 presents evidence that contradicts the concession the writer makes in paragraph 3 about changed work patterns and distant warehouse jobs
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Paragraph 4 offers no evidence about work patterns; the concession in paragraph 3 that 'the old pattern is gone' stands unchallenged throughout the essay.

items.stem: Which of the following best evaluates the contribution of paragraph 5 to the argument as a whole?

options.text: It introduces a new criticism of the methods Weil used to gather his figures in six counties, faulting his small sample of stations
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The writer never questions Weil's reporting methods or sample; paragraph 2 calls the reporting 'the book's great strength.'

options.text: It qualifies the writer's claim by acknowledging that the levy imposed real costs on Tillery County households that many could not afford
options.label: reversal
options.why: Paragraph 5 minimizes the cost as 'roughly the price of a tank of gas,' which strengthens rather than qualifies the writer's case.

options.text: It answers the question posed at the end of paragraph 4 with a counterexample, giving the final verdict a factual basis
options.label: correct
options.why: Paragraph 4 ends by asking what happens when the county buys the truck; paragraph 5 reports Tillery County's levy and roster growth, which paragraph 6's claim that starvation 'has a remedy' depends on.

options.text: It summarizes the book's strongest reporting so that the reader can weigh its warning fairly before the conclusion, recalling his aging rosters
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Paragraph 5 presents the writer's own evidence from Tillery County, which she calls 'more hopeful than Weil allows'; it is not a summary of the book.

items.stem: In paragraph 6, the writer's phrase "when it reaches for the obituary" primarily serves to

options.text: concede that the volunteer model is in fact beyond saving while urging readers to admire its final years
options.label: reversal
options.why: Paragraph 6 explicitly affirms that the service's starvation has a remedy and tells county boards it is 'in your budget.'

options.text: characterize Weil's conclusion as a premature death notice, reinforcing the contrast between natural decline and preventable neglect
options.label: correct
options.why: 'Obituary' frames Weil's diagnosis of obsolescence as declaring a death; paragraph 6 then insists the service is 'not dying of old age' but 'being starved,' a condition with a remedy.

options.text: suggest that the book memorializes, by name, volunteers who died answering calls alone in understaffed counties
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: The literal sense of 'obituary' is not in play; the book's described content concerns aging rosters and dissolved companies, not deaths in service.

options.text: mock the book's somber tone as melodramatic, undercutting the praise offered in the preceding sentence
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Paragraph 6 calls the portraits 'honest and often moving' and the warning 'overdue'; the writer disputes the diagnosis, not the seriousness of the tone.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the writer's overall stance toward Siren on the Ridge?

options.text: Admiration for its reporting combined with a rejection of the conclusion it draws from that reporting
options.label: correct
options.why: Paragraph 2 calls the reporting 'the book's great strength,' paragraph 3 says 'Where the book falters is in its diagnosis,' and paragraph 6 tells readers to read it for its portraits but 'skeptically when it reaches for the obituary.'

options.text: Gratitude that the book finally documents a crisis, paired with doubt that its figures are accurate
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The writer never questions Weil's numbers; she accepts them as 'the shape of the thing' and disputes only what they mean.

options.text: Respect for its honest portraits, paired with regret that it offers no concrete policy recommendation
options.label: reversal
options.why: Weil does make a recommendation, that counties 'hire paid crews'; the writer objects to that recommendation rather than to its absence.

options.text: Approval of its warning about aging rosters along with a sense that its tone is too sentimental
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The writer praises the volunteers' 'flat, unsentimental voices' and calls the portraits 'honest'; she faults the book's diagnosis, not its emotional register.

items.stem: In paragraph 5, the writer's decision to describe the Tillery County levy as 'roughly the price of a tank of gas per household per year' is most effective for the intended audience because it

options.text: frames the proposed remedy as a cost small enough that budget-minded officials could adopt it without political risk
options.label: correct
options.why: The passage is aimed at county commissioners who control budgets (sentences 4 and 29); translating the levy into a familiar, modest household expense answers their likely objection about cost.

options.text: reminds commissioners that fuel costs are themselves a major expense in rural fire service
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: The tank of gas is a unit of comparison for the levy's size, not a reference to the fire company's fuel costs, which the passage never mentions.

options.text: suggests that households, rather than county boards, should take responsibility for funding equipment
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer's whole argument is that the county, 'not the fish fry,' should buy the truck; the per-household figure describes a public levy, not private donations.

options.text: demonstrates that Tillery County is wealthier than the writer's own county and so can afford more
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Nothing in the passage compares the wealth of the two counties; the figure stresses how little the levy costs anyone.

items.stem: The passage can best be understood as a response to which of the following situations?

options.text: A newly published book that documents shrinking volunteer rosters and urges counties to replace volunteers with paid crews
options.label: correct
options.why: Paragraph 1 identifies 'Conrad Weil's new book' as the occasion, and paragraph 3 summarizes its argument that counties should 'hire paid crews.'

options.text: A proposal before the Brannock County board to dissolve the Marrow Creek Volunteer Fire Company
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The dissolved township company is one of Weil's examples; nothing indicates that Marrow Creek faces such a proposal.

options.text: A recent state decision to raise the certified training requirement for new recruits
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: The training increase is evidence within paragraph 3, not the occasion for writing; the writer says it rose from forty hours 'when I joined,' not recently.

options.text: The passage of a fire levy in a neighboring county that the writer wants her own county to copy
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The Tillery levy is a counterexample offered as evidence in paragraph 5; the passage opens and closes around Weil's book, not the levy.

items.stem: In paragraph 3, the detail that the state 'now requires one hundred eighty hours of certified training before a recruit may enter a burning building, up from forty when I joined' is offered primarily as evidence for which claim?

options.text: The volunteer system has been 'quietly loaded with burdens it was never designed to carry'
options.label: correct
options.why: The training detail immediately follows sentence 13 and is the first of two burdens (training, then self-funded equipment) illustrating that claim.

options.text: The volunteer model is 'simply obsolete' because workers no longer live near the station
options.label: reversal
options.why: This is Weil's diagnosis, which the writer is rebutting; the training hours support her counter-explanation, not his.

options.text: 'The people were there all along' but had been 'priced out of serving'
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: That claim appears in paragraph 5 and is supported by the Tillery County roster figures, not by the training requirement.

options.text: Weil's reporting is the book's 'great strength' because its figures are so grim
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The training figure comes from the writer's own experience, not from Weil's reporting, and it serves her critique rather than her praise.

items.stem: In paragraph 3, the writer's statement that 'I grant that the old pattern is gone; nobody leaves a shift at a distribution warehouse forty miles away to answer a brush fire' functions primarily to

options.text: accept the factual basis of Weil's argument in order to isolate and dispute the conclusion he draws from it
options.label: correct
options.why: The concession admits the changed work pattern Weil describes, and the next sentence pivots with 'But obsolete is the wrong word,' narrowing the disagreement to the diagnosis.

options.text: concede that the volunteer model cannot survive and shift the argument toward how paid crews should be funded
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer explicitly denies that the model is obsolete and never endorses paid crews; the concession is limited to the work pattern.

options.text: illustrate with a vivid example how far volunteers now commute, reinforcing Weil's point about distance
options.label: partially_right
options.why: The example is vivid, but its purpose is to set up the rebuttal that follows, not to strengthen Weil's case.

options.text: signal that the writer's own experience is dated and that Weil's more recent reporting should be trusted
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The writer goes on to cite her own experience of training hours and fundraising as authoritative; nothing suggests she defers to Weil.

items.stem: Which of the following best evaluates how the comparison to 'asking a lifeguard to run a lemonade stand to pay for the pool' in paragraph 4 advances the writer's purpose?

options.text: It transfers a familiar arrangement into a setting where its unfairness is immediately visible, preparing the reader to see fundraising as a structural failure
options.label: correct
options.why: Sentence 19 says 'The absurdity would be obvious anywhere else,' and sentence 20 then names fundraising 'the structural failure it is'; the analogy makes a normalized burden look absurd.

options.text: It lightens the tone after the grim statistics of paragraph 2, reassuring readers that the crisis is less serious than Weil suggests
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The writer never minimizes the crisis; she calls Weil's warning 'overdue' and uses the analogy to sharpen criticism, not to reassure.

options.text: It provides a second case study that, like Tillery County, shows what happens when public money covers equipment
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The lifeguard is a hypothetical comparison, not evidence; the only case study is Tillery County in paragraph 5.

options.text: It demonstrates that fire companies, like pools, should charge the public user fees for the protection they provide
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The analogy ridicules making the lifeguard raise pool money; it argues against self-funding, not for fees.

items.stem: The sentence 'Where the book falters is in its diagnosis' at the opening of paragraph 3 primarily serves to

options.text: mark the turn from praise to critique while confining the disagreement to Weil's interpretation rather than his facts
options.label: correct
options.why: It follows paragraph 2's praise of the reporting and introduces the critique; the word 'diagnosis' limits the objection to Weil's reading of the evidence, which the rest of the paragraph pursues.

options.text: announce that the writer will now dispute the accuracy of the numbers reported in paragraph 2
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer never challenges the figures; she treats them as 'the shape of the thing' and attacks only the conclusion drawn from them.

options.text: summarize the argument of paragraphs 1 and 2 before introducing the Tillery County evidence
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: The sentence looks forward to the critique in paragraph 3, not to the evidence in paragraph 5, and it summarizes nothing.

options.text: soften the criticism that follows by acknowledging that every book has minor weaknesses
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The sentence is blunt rather than softening, and the flaw it names, the diagnosis, is the book's central argument, not a minor weakness.

items.stem: Paragraph 2 develops its point primarily through

options.text: accumulating specific figures and cases from Weil's reporting to show that the decline is widespread rather than local
options.label: correct
options.why: The paragraph lists the age shift, roster shrinkage, the lone chief, and the dissolved township, then concludes 'These are not isolated anecdotes; they are the shape of the thing.'

options.text: contrasting the writer's own department with the departments Weil visited in other states
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The writer's department does not appear in paragraph 2; the examples all come from Weil's six counties.

options.text: tracing a chain of causes that explains why rosters have aged and shrunk over twenty years
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Paragraph 2 describes the decline without explaining it; causal explanation begins in paragraph 3 with training and fundraising burdens.

options.text: defining what counts as a functioning fire company and measuring each station against it
options.label: unsupported
options.why: No definition or standard is offered; the paragraph relies on reported numbers and portraits.

items.stem: In paragraph 3, the structure of the sentence 'We lost them because we asked each one to be a firefighter, a fundraiser, a mechanic, and a grant writer, and then wondered why only retirees had the hours' emphasizes the writer's point chiefly by

options.text: stacking the roles in a series before the final clause, so that the bewilderment it describes seems unwarranted
options.label: correct
options.why: The four-item list piles up the demands, and the delayed 'and then wondered' lands after the pile, exposing the gap between what was asked and the surprise at the result.

options.text: placing the cause first and the effect last to suggest the loss of volunteers was unforeseeable
options.label: reversal
options.why: The sentence implies the opposite: given the demands listed, the outcome should have been obvious.

options.text: balancing two independent clauses of equal weight to present apathy and overwork as competing explanations
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Apathy is rejected in the previous sentence; this sentence offers a single explanation, not two balanced alternatives.

options.text: repeating the word 'we' to shift blame onto the volunteers themselves for taking on too much
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: 'We' refers to the community and system that made demands, and the blame falls on the burdens imposed, not on the volunteers.

items.stem: In paragraph 1, the semicolon in 'Some nights that is nine people; some nights it is three' primarily serves to

options.text: set two matched clauses side by side so the gap between the turnouts conveys how unpredictable a response can be
options.label: correct
options.why: The semicolon joins parallel clauses without a connecting word, letting the contrast between nine and three stand starkly and illustrating the 'arithmetic' the writer says Weil understands.

options.text: subordinate the second clause to the first, implying that three responders is the more typical turnout
options.label: convention_error
options.why: A semicolon links independent clauses of equal weight; neither clause is subordinated, and the sentence gives no sense of which turnout is typical.

options.text: introduce an explanation of why fewer volunteers appear on certain nights
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: No explanation follows the semicolon, only a second instance; causes are not discussed until paragraph 3.

options.text: create a pause that signals the writer's shift from personal memory to discussion of the book
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: The shift to the book occurs in the next sentence, not at the semicolon, which sits inside a description of turnout.

blueprint.speaker: Imogen Tarrow, a former volunteer maintainer of a small text-parsing library for nine years, now writing criticism for a general-interest quarterly
blueprint.audience: Educated general readers of a literary and ideas quarterly, most of whom use software built on volunteer-maintained libraries without knowing it, including managers and engineers at the institutions that depend on such code
blueprint.exigence: The publication of Desmond Alcock's book Nobody's Job, which opens with the recent collapse of thousands of websites after the lone maintainer of the tidyclock library deleted it
blueprint.purpose: To recommend the book's diagnosis of fragile volunteer infrastructure while rejecting its prescribed cure of corporate sponsorship, and to propose instead that dependent institutions contribute maintenance labor
blueprint.context: A review essay in The Harrowgate Quarterly, written shortly after a widely noticed outage caused by a single volunteer quitting
blueprint.claim: Alcock is right that critical software rests on unseen, unpaid individuals, but wrong that money is the remedy; the obligation to maintain should attach to dependence and be paid in hours by the institutions that rely on the code.
blueprint.line_of_reasoning: Paragraph 1 opens with the tidyclock anecdote and establishes the reviewer's ethos as a former maintainer. Paragraph 2 endorses the book's diagnosis (survey, load-bearing-walls metaphor). Paragraph 3 pivots to the book's prescription, concedes that money has helped, then rebuts with the shoveling analogy: payment converts a gift into a contract. Paragraph 4 shifts to personal testimony about ungrateful bug reports to show that the real deficit is recognition, not cash, and links that back to the critique. Paragraph 5 supplies the alternative cure (institutions lending hours, volunteer fire department analogy) with a qualification of its limits. Paragraph 6 renders the verdict and returns to the schoolteacher of the opening.

devices.function: Opens with the concrete tidyclock collapse to dramatize the stakes and introduce the book's starting point
Establishes the reviewer's standing as a former maintainer who reads the book from inside the problem
Reports Alcock's survey finding to support the diagnosis that most heavily used packages depend on one volunteer
Load-bearing walls figure the hidden, unexamined dependence of institutions on volunteer code; returned to in the proposal to spread the weight
Colons set up the explanation of the metaphor and the statement of Alcock's remedy
Very short sentences after long ones isolate key points: no one chose the arrangement; only one thank-you
Shift from appreciative to critical at paragraph 3, then from analytical to personal and wry at paragraph 4
Grants that stipends have saved projects before rebutting that payment changes the nature of the work
Shoveling the shared walkway shows how payment converts a gift into a service; volunteer fire departments model obligation attached to dependence
Gift versus contract, hours versus dollars, frighten versus comfort sharpen the reviewer's distinctions
Presses readers to recognize that they may have treated a person as a department
The one-word sentence One. wryly registers the scarcity of gratitude without complaint
Limits the proposal's scope so it cannot be dismissed as a cure-all
Instructs the reader how to read the book, delivering the verdict
Parallel clauses build the consequences of payment and balance the two halves of the verdict

blueprint.counterargument: Alcock's position, and the reviewer's own concession, that corporate sponsorship money has in fact rescued projects such as an encryption library; the reviewer grants this and rebuts that payment turns a gift into a contract shaped by the sponsor's priorities.

provenance.note: Original review essay of a fictional book, Nobody's Job, by the fictional author Desmond Alcock. All people, institutions, libraries and figures are invented.

g-lr01.title: Standing on Her Work
paragraphs: One Tuesday last October, a date-formatting library called tidyclock vanished from the public package registry, and by morning several thousand websites could no longer tell their users what day it was.
Its sole maintainer, a retired schoolteacher in Pell Harbor, had deleted it after a decade of unpaid work and one rude bug report too many.
Desmond Alcock's new book, Nobody's Job, opens with that night, and it is the right place to begin.
I spent nine years maintaining a small text-parsing library used by companies I was never allowed to name, so I read Alcock with the uneasy attention of a patient reading her own chart.
The book's first half is a diagnosis, and it is a good one.
Alcock surveyed four hundred of the most heavily downloaded packages in three programming languages and found that more than half depended on a single active volunteer.

He calls these projects load-bearing walls that no inspector has visited, and the metaphor earns its keep: the walls are hidden inside the plaster of every bank, hospital, and school district that runs code on top of them.
Nobody chose this arrangement.
It accreted, one convenient download at a time, until the whole structure rested on the patience of people who could stop at any moment and owed us nothing if they did.
It is in the second half, where Alcock turns from diagnosis to cure, that the book loses its footing.
His remedy is sponsorship: corporations that profit from open-source software should fund its maintainers, and he describes several foundations that already do so.
I will grant that money has saved projects.
A stipend kept at least one widely used encryption library alive after its maintainer nearly quit, and Alcock tells that story well.
But a stipend changes what the work is.

Consider the neighbor who shovels the shared walkway every winter because no one else will; the day you start paying her, the shoveling becomes a service, the snow becomes her problem, and you acquire the right to complain about ice.
Sponsorship converts a gift into a contract, and the contract arrives written in the sponsor's priorities, not the project's.
I know something about how such gifts are received.

In nine years I received roughly four thousand bug reports, most of them phrased as demands, several of them threatening, and one, from a hospital network in a city I have never visited, that began with the words "thank you."
One.
Did any of those four thousand correspondents imagine that a person, rather than a department, was reading them at eleven at night?
Alcock understands this loneliness better than any writer I have read, which is precisely why his faith in a check is so puzzling.
The better cure is already visible in the margins of his own book, though he never names it.
The institutions that depend on these libraries do not lack money; they lack a sense that the maintenance is theirs to do.
A regional bank runs tidyclock on its login page, employs ninety engineers, and has never assigned one of them a Friday afternoon to review tidyclock's open issues.
Volunteer fire departments survive not because the town mails a check to the one person who owns a hose but because the people whose houses would burn show up for the drills.
The obligation should attach to dependence, not to profit, and it should be paid in hours, not dollars.
This will not rescue every project, and the smallest libraries will still rely on the stubbornness of individuals; but it would spread the weight across the walls that bear it.
Nobody's Job deserves the wide readership it will probably get.
Read it for the first half, which will frighten you in the right way, and argue with the second, which will comfort you in the wrong one.
The retired schoolteacher in Pell Harbor did not need a sponsor.
She needed the several thousand of us who were standing on her work to notice that we were.

items.stem: The writer's account in paragraph 4 of the bug reports she received over nine years is most likely intended to affect readers by

options.text: suggesting that maintainers are too easily wounded by ordinary criticism to be trusted with the critical infrastructure that institutions depend on
options.label: reversal
options.why: The passage's sympathy runs toward maintainers and against those who make demands of them; it faults the dependents, not the volunteers.

options.text: demonstrating that hospital networks are more considerate users of volunteer code than the banks or corporations that send most reports
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: The single hospital thank-you is used as a rarity, not as a comparison among institutional types; the passage never ranks hospitals against banks or says who sends most reports.

options.text: establishing the technical authority she needs, as a nine-year maintainer, to challenge the findings and methods of Alcock's survey
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: She does not challenge the survey; she endorses the diagnosis in paragraph 2. The anecdote concerns recognition and loneliness, not technical credentials.

options.text: prompting them to recognize that they, too, may have treated an individual volunteer as if she were an anonymous department
options.label: correct
options.why: The account of demanding reports is followed by a question asking whether any correspondent imagined 'a person, rather than a department' was reading them, and the essay closes by naming 'the several thousand of us who were standing on her work'; the audience of ordinary users is being implicated in the neglect.

items.stem: In paragraph 3, the sentence beginning "A stipend kept at least one widely used encryption library alive" functions primarily as

options.text: evidence supporting the writer's concession that sponsorship money has in fact rescued some projects
options.label: correct
options.why: It directly follows 'I will grant that money has saved projects' and supplies a specific case of a stipend saving a library, before the rebuttal 'But a stipend changes what the work is.'

options.text: evidence supporting the writer's claim that obligations should be paid in hours rather than dollars
options.label: reversal
options.why: The example shows money working, which is the opposite of the hours-not-dollars claim; it belongs to the conceded point, not the writer's own remedy.

options.text: evidence that the second half of the book is better written than the first
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Although the writer notes Alcock 'tells that story well,' she has just said the second half 'loses its footing' and never compares the prose quality of the two halves.

options.text: a claim that Alcock's survey of four hundred packages underestimates the role of foundations
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The sentence reports a specific case rather than asserting a general position, and it says nothing about the survey's accuracy.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the relationship between paragraph 2 and paragraph 3?

options.text: Paragraph 2 endorses the book's diagnosis of the problem, and paragraph 3 rejects the book's proposed cure
options.label: correct
options.why: Paragraph 2 opens 'The book's first half is a diagnosis, and it is a good one,' and paragraph 3 opens by locating the book's failure 'in the second half, where Alcock turns from diagnosis to cure.'

options.text: Paragraph 2 raises a problem, and paragraph 3 presents the writer's own solution to it
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Paragraph 3 examines and rebuts Alcock's solution; the writer's own solution does not appear until paragraph 5.

options.text: Paragraph 2 states the writer's own thesis, and paragraph 3 supplies further evidence supporting that thesis
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Paragraph 2 summarizes Alcock's findings rather than the writer's thesis, and paragraph 3 turns against the book rather than supporting what precedes it.

options.text: Paragraph 2 praises the book's survey, and paragraph 3 shows that the survey's findings were flawed
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer never questions the survey; she continues to accept the diagnosis and later says the first half 'will frighten you in the right way.'

items.stem: The sentence "Alcock understands this loneliness better than any writer I have read, which is precisely why his faith in a check is so puzzling" primarily serves to

options.text: convey the writer's contempt for a critic who has never maintained software himself and so cannot grasp what volunteer maintainers endure
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The sentence credits Alcock with unmatched understanding; its tone is puzzled and respectful, and the passage never says Alcock lacks maintenance experience or fails to grasp maintainers' situation.

options.text: return the personal testimony of paragraph 4 to the evaluation of the book by tying the lack of recognition to the inadequacy of sponsorship
options.label: correct
options.why: After the digression into her own bug reports, the sentence names Alcock again and uses 'this loneliness' to connect the anecdote's point about being unseen to the critique that money cannot address it, preparing the alternative cure in paragraph 5.

options.text: soften the review's criticism by conceding that Alcock's empathy outweighs the weakness of his remedy, so that the second half of the book seems largely redeemed
options.label: partially_right
options.why: The praise of Alcock's understanding is real, but the sentence uses it to sharpen, not soften, the objection: his insight makes the remedy 'puzzling,' and the second half is never redeemed.

options.text: introduce the writer's own proposal that the institutions depending on these libraries should contribute engineers' hours instead of corporate sponsorship money
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The proposal is introduced in the next paragraph with 'The better cure is already visible'; this sentence only diagnoses the mismatch in Alcock's thinking.

items.stem: The effect of the one-word sentence "One." in paragraph 4 is best described as

options.text: expressing open anger at the hospital network that waited so long, nearly nine years, to finally thank her
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The hospital is the one correspondent who did thank her; the passage directs no anger at it and gives no timing for its message, and the restraint of a single word is the opposite of open anger.

options.text: emphasizing that only one institution, a hospital network in a distant city, was actually using the writer's library
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: The 'one' counts thank-you messages, not users; the previous sentence establishes thousands of correspondents, and paragraph 1 refers to companies she could not name.

options.text: isolating the number with wry understatement so that the rarity of gratitude registers more sharply than any complaint could
options.label: correct
options.why: The word follows a long sentence cataloguing four thousand demanding reports; its brevity sets the single thank-you apart, and the flat restatement without commentary is understated rather than indignant.

options.text: establishing the writer's credibility by showing she kept precise, dated records of every report she received over nine years
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The passage says 'roughly four thousand,' signalling approximation; the short sentence is about scarcity of thanks, not record-keeping.

items.stem: Taken together, the references to "every bank, hospital, and school district" in paragraph 2 and to "the several thousand of us who were standing on her work" in paragraph 6 suggest that the writer imagines her audience primarily as

options.text: people who benefit from volunteer-maintained code without having recognized that dependence
options.label: correct
options.why: The institutions named in paragraph 2 are those that unknowingly run code on hidden walls, and the closing sentence counts the reader among the thousands who failed to notice they were standing on the schoolteacher's work.

options.text: volunteer maintainers who have themselves considered deleting projects after abusive bug reports
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: The writer is a former maintainer, but she addresses the dependent many, not the lone maintainers; the closing sentence places readers among those standing on the work, not among those doing it.

options.text: corporate executives who already fund open-source foundations and want their money spent well
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Sponsoring foundations are Alcock's proposed remedy, which the writer rejects; nothing frames the reader as an existing sponsor.

options.text: readers of Alcock's book who have already accepted his argument and need to be talked out of it
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Paragraph 6 tells readers to read the book, implying they have not yet; the writer anticipates rather than corrects their response.

items.stem: The comparison to volunteer fire departments in paragraph 5 is most likely intended to appeal to the audience's

options.text: belief that people exposed to a shared danger owe one another participation rather than payment
options.label: correct
options.why: The analogy stresses that the people whose houses would burn show up for drills instead of mailing a check, modeling the claim that obligation should attach to dependence and be paid in hours.

options.text: admiration for individuals who continue dangerous unpaid work out of personal stubbornness
options.label: reversal
options.why: The analogy rejects reliance on the one person who owns a hose; stubborn individuals are what the writer wants to stop depending on.

options.text: distrust of small towns that neglect essential services until an emergency forces action
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The fire department is presented as a successful model, not as an example of neglect.

options.text: assumption that institutions with ninety engineers can easily afford modest sponsorship stipends
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The bank example concerns a failure to assign hours, and the fire department analogy argues against checks, not for affordable ones.

items.stem: Which of the following sentences from the passage most directly states the writer's central claim?

options.text: "The obligation should attach to dependence, not to profit, and it should be paid in hours, not dollars."
options.label: correct
options.why: This sentence states the writer's own prescription, which the whole review builds toward and which the closing return to the schoolteacher restates.

options.text: "The book's first half is a diagnosis, and it is a good one."
options.label: partially_right
options.why: This endorses only the diagnosis; the review's distinctive claim concerns the cure, which this sentence does not address.

options.text: "Sponsorship converts a gift into a contract, and the contract arrives written in the sponsor's priorities, not the project's."
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: This is the rebuttal of Alcock's remedy, a supporting step, but it does not state what the writer proposes instead.

options.text: "Nobody's Job deserves the wide readership it will probably get."
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: This is the reviewer's verdict on the book's merit, not the argumentative claim about where maintenance obligation lies.

items.stem: In paragraph 5, the sentence beginning "This will not rescue every project" primarily serves to

options.text: limit the reach of the proposal so that it cannot be dismissed for failing to solve every case
options.label: correct
options.why: The writer concedes that the smallest libraries will still depend on individuals, then reasserts the proposal's main benefit of spreading the weight; the qualification preempts an objection.

options.text: concede that Alcock's sponsorship model remains necessary for the smallest and most neglected libraries
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The sentence says small libraries will rely on individual stubbornness; it does not reintroduce sponsorship as a fallback.

options.text: signal that the writer has come to doubt whether institutions will contribute hours at all
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The sentence ends with a confident claim that the proposal would spread the weight; it qualifies scope, not conviction.

options.text: return to the load-bearing metaphor in order to restate the diagnosis offered in paragraph 2
options.label: partially_right
options.why: The sentence does reuse the wall image, but its purpose is to bound and defend the cure, not to restate the diagnosis.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes how the passage's overall thesis is organized?

options.text: An endorsement of the book's diagnosis, a rejection of its proposed cure, and a substitute remedy
options.label: correct
options.why: Paragraph 2 praises the diagnosis, paragraphs 3 and 4 reject sponsorship, paragraph 5 offers hours instead of dollars, and paragraph 6 compresses this into read the first half, argue with the second.

options.text: A summary of the book's evidence, a defense of its conclusions, and a call for a wider readership
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer disputes rather than defends the book's conclusions about the cure; only the diagnosis is accepted.
