options.text: A personal account of maintaining software, a critique of corporate funders, and a plea for gratitude
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: The personal account supports the argument but is not its spine, and the proposal concerns assigned hours, not gratitude from users.

options.text: A description of the tidyclock outage, an analysis of its causes, and a prediction that it will recur
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: The outage frames the review, but the passage argues about remedies rather than predicting repetition.

items.stem: The writer's assertion in paragraph 5 that the better cure is "visible in the margins of his own book, though he never names it" is most effective at

options.text: presenting her alternative as consistent with Alcock's own evidence rather than as a rejection of his project
options.label: correct
options.why: By locating the cure inside the book, the writer frames her disagreement as completing Alcock's work with his own material, which keeps her praise of the first half credible.

options.text: suggesting that Alcock deliberately suppressed a conclusion that would have displeased corporate sponsors
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Nothing in the passage attributes motive or suppression to Alcock; the writer calls his faith in a check puzzling, not dishonest.

options.text: conceding that her proposal is less original than Alcock's and therefore less likely to be adopted
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Locating the cure in his margins does not weaken her proposal; the writer calls it the better cure and argues for it confidently.

options.text: retracting her earlier judgment that the second half of the book loses its footing
options.label: reversal
options.why: The sentence introduces the alternative to Alcock's cure; it sustains, rather than withdraws, the criticism of the second half.

items.stem: The writer's use of the neighbor who shovels the shared walkway in paragraph 3 primarily advances her purpose by

options.text: rendering an abstract claim about payment and obligation in a scene readers can test against their own experience
options.label: correct
options.why: The analogy makes concrete the claim that a stipend changes what the work is, showing how paying converts a gift into a service and gives the payer the right to complain.

options.text: supplying a documented case in which sponsorship caused a volunteer to abandon a project
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The neighbor is a hypothetical illustration, not a documented case, and the neighbor does not quit; the point is the changed relationship.

options.text: proving that maintainers would refuse payment if it were offered to them
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The analogy says nothing about refusal; the writer even grants that stipends have saved projects.

options.text: contrasting neighborly generosity with the hostility of the bug reports described in paragraph 4
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: The analogy is about what payment does to a gift, and it precedes the bug report testimony rather than contrasting with it.

items.stem: In paragraph 5, the writer develops the claim that institutions "lack a sense that the maintenance is theirs to do" chiefly through

options.text: a hypothetical example of a single institution followed by a comparison to a familiar civic practice
options.label: correct
options.why: The regional bank with ninety engineers illustrates the missing sense of ownership, and the volunteer fire department supplies the model of what ownership looks like.

options.text: a sequence of causes tracing how convenient downloads accumulated into a fragile structure
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: That causal account of accretion appears in paragraph 2, not in the development of paragraph 5.

options.text: a survey statistic showing how few engineers at dependent firms review open issues
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: The only survey statistic is Alcock's in paragraph 2 about packages, and the bank example gives no survey figure about engineers.

options.text: a personal anecdote about a bank that once ignored her requests for assistance
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The bank is a generic illustration of a login page running tidyclock, not an episode from the writer's own history.

items.stem: In paragraph 3, the structure of the clause "the day you start paying her, the shoveling becomes a service, the snow becomes her problem, and you acquire the right to complain about ice" chiefly emphasizes

options.text: how a single act of payment sets off a chain of consequences that ends with the payer entitled to complain
options.label: correct
options.why: The introductory time clause marks the one triggering moment, and the three parallel main clauses accumulate consequences, with the final one landing on the payer's new entitlement.

options.text: how the neighbor's labor grows heavier with each winter that she is left to shovel alone
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The clauses describe changes in the relationship after payment, not increasing physical labor over years.

options.text: how a service, a problem, and a right are three separate benefits the neighbor gains from being paid
options.label: reversal
options.why: Only the last clause names a right, and it belongs to the payer, not the neighbor; the series records losses of the gift character, not benefits.

options.text: how uncertain it is whether the neighbor will continue shoveling once money is involved
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The parallel declaratives are flatly certain; nothing in the structure conveys doubt about continuation.

items.stem: The writer's choice of the first-person plural in "owed us nothing" in paragraph 2 and "the several thousand of us" in paragraph 6 is most effective because it

options.text: places the writer alongside her readers among those responsible, so the proposal reads as shared duty rather than accusation
options.label: correct
options.why: By counting herself among the dependents who failed to notice, the writer turns the final charge into a collective admission, which suits an argument that obligation attaches to dependence.

options.text: separates the writer and other maintainers from the institutions that profit from their unpaid labor
options.label: reversal
options.why: The pronoun includes the writer with the dependents who were standing on the work, not with the maintainers set apart from them.

options.text: directs the closing sentences specifically at Alcock as the one reader most in need of correction
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: The plural widens the address to everyone who ran code on the walls; Alcock is not singled out in these sentences.

options.text: softens the review's criticism by implying that the writer herself once favored corporate sponsorship
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Nothing suggests the writer ever favored sponsorship; the shared failing is not noticing dependence, not endorsing a check.

blueprint.speaker: Imogen Halvorsen, a retired schoolteacher and amateur family historian in the fictional mill town of Carrow Bend, who has kept her grandmother's household ledgers and letters
blueprint.audience: Readers of a community magazine, mostly parents and grandparents, who have just received the public library's 'Screens Down at Supper' pledge card
blueprint.exigence: The Carrow Bend Public Library's pledge drive asks households to put screens away at supper 'to give your children back the table'; the writer agrees with the practice but objects to the wording, which casts children as the problem
blueprint.purpose: To persuade readers to sign the pledge but to reframe it as a shared household ritual that binds adults as much as children, using three generations of family history as evidence
blueprint.context: A historical-narrative essay published in a small-town quarterly magazine; the writer narrates her family's responses to the arrival of the radio (1938), the telephone (1954) and the television (1967) and draws a lesson for the present
blueprint.claim: Every generation has had to fence off the supper hour from a new machine, and the fences that held were rituals kept by the whole household, not curfews imposed on the young; the difference between a curfew and a ritual matters more than the hour chosen
blueprint.line_of_reasoning: P1 presents the occasion (the pledge card) and the writer's unease with its wording, posed as questions. P2 narrates the 1938 radio anecdote, revealing that the grandfather, not the children, was the problem and that the rule applied to everyone. P3 enumerates the telephone and television to show the household's response was a repeated pattern: schedule the machine, do not banish it. P4 supplies the conceptual distinction between a curfew and a ritual, with the mill-whistle analogy, reinterpreting the narrated examples. P5 concedes that the ledgers record sullen suppers, narrowing the claim from 'the hour produced conversation' to 'the hour produced attendance,' then rebuts by arguing attendance is itself the lasting good. P6 returns to the pledge card with direct exhortation, instructing readers to cross out the second line, and closes with two clipped sentences.
evidence_types: analogy to the town mill whistle

devices.function: Voices the writer's objection to the card's wording and frames the essay's inquiry into who actually abandons the table
Narrates the grandmother's 1938 radio rule as the founding example that the rule bound adults as much as children
The ledger's precise price lends documentary credibility to the family story
Colons set off the ledger's rule and the household's recurring response for emphasis
The fence, the stranger at the door, and the whistle versus warrant recast the rule as a shared boundary rather than a punishment
The telephone cord coiled like a sleeping cat renders the device domesticated and harmless once scheduled
Parallel 'In 1954... In 1967...' and 'stayed; stayed; stayed' stress the repetition of the pattern across machines
Each machine as a stranger who must be told when to call makes scheduling, not banning, the natural response
'heaven help us' wryly admits the television's permanence while keeping the tone light
Distinguishes curfew (imposed, with suspect and warden) from ritual (done together on purpose) to name the essay's central distinction
Opposed pairs sharpen the contrast between imposed rule and shared practice and between changing machines and the unchanging fence
The noon mill whistle, heard by all as a shared stop rather than an accusation, models how the supper rule should feel
'I think' softens the assertion and marks the writer's reasoning as considered rather than dogmatic
Admits the suppers were often sullen, narrows the claim to attendance, then argues attendance is what memory retains
Very short sentences after long ones ('But attendance, it turns out, is not nothing'; 'The machine has changed. The fence has not.') create emphasis and finality
Sets the vividly remembered sullen suppers against the unremembered evenings with the set on
Turns to readers with imperatives, enlisting them as the adults the rule must include
Shifts from uneasy questioning to wry narration, then to candid concession, then to assured exhortation

blueprint.counterargument: That the quiet hour did not actually produce warm family conversation; the ledgers and letters show sullen, silent meals. The writer concedes this fully, narrows the claim to attendance, and rebuts by observing that the sullen suppers are the ones remembered in detail while the evenings with the set on left no memory at all.

provenance.note: Entirely fictional writer, town, library, ledgers and figures; composed for practice-exam use.

g-lr08.title: A Fence Around an Hour
paragraphs: The pledge card came in the same envelope as the library's autumn newsletter, printed on oatmeal-colored stock with a line for each member of the household to sign.
"Screens Down at Supper," it read, and underneath, in smaller type, "Give your children back the table."
I read it twice at my own kitchen table, phone face down beside the sugar bowl, and felt the particular unease of someone who agrees with a proposal and distrusts its wording.
Give the children back the table?
Who, exactly, had taken it from them?

My grandmother, Solveig Arnesen, bought her first radio in the autumn of 1938, a walnut cabinet set that cost her, according to the household ledger she kept in a looping hand, thirty-one dollars and forty cents.
The ledger records the purchase on a Tuesday.
By the following Sunday a second entry appears, not a sum but a sentence: "No set from six to seven. All of us."

The family story is that my grandfather, not the children, had been the trouble, sitting with his ear to the speaker through an entire meal while the program crackled about grain prices and a prizefight in a city none of them would ever see.
The rule she wrote was not a punishment for the young.
It was a fence she built around an hour, and she built it to keep herself and her husband inside as much as anyone.
The pattern repeated itself with a regularity that would be comic if it were not so instructive.
In 1954 the telephone arrived, and my mother remembers the cord unplugged at a quarter to six and coiled on top of the icebox like a sleeping cat.
In 1967 the television came, and with it a new entry in a new ledger, this time in my mother's hand: "Set off at supper, no exceptions, Dad included."
Each machine was a stranger at the door, and each time the household did the same thing: it did not bar the stranger, it told the stranger when to call.
The radio stayed; the telephone stayed; the television, heaven help us, stayed.
What changed was that a single hour was marked off as belonging to the people at the table rather than to the voices coming through the wall.
There is a difference, I think, between a curfew and a ritual, and the difference matters more than the hour chosen.
A curfew is a rule imposed on someone by someone else; it names a suspect and a warden.
A ritual is a thing a group does together, on purpose, at a set time, because doing it together is the point.
The mill at the foot of Carrow Bend used to blow its whistle at noon, and nobody heard that whistle as an accusation; it was simply the sound of everyone stopping at once.
My grandmother's "All of us" was a whistle, not a warrant.
I will concede that the ledgers do not record a single happy supper.

They record cabbage and coal and the price of shoes, and the surviving letters mention more than one meal eaten in a silence that was sullen rather than peaceful, teenagers and tired parents with nothing to say and a forbidden radio in the next room.
Nostalgia would have me believe that the quiet hour produced conversation; the evidence suggests only that it produced attendance.
But attendance, it turns out, is not nothing.
The sullen suppers of 1941 are the ones my mother still describes in detail, down to the pattern on the oilcloth, and she cannot describe a single evening when the set was on.
So I will sign the card, and I would urge you to sign it as well, though I would ask you to take a pen and cross out the second line before you do.
Do not give the children back the table.
Sit down at it yourself, phone in the drawer, and let them see you, every night, until the hour belongs to all of you and nobody remembers whom it was meant to protect.
My grandmother knew this in 1938 with a radio she could barely afford.
The machine has changed.
The fence has not.

items.stem: In paragraph 2, the writer's emphasis that her grandfather, "not the children, had been the trouble" most likely appeals to the audience by

options.text: reassuring parents that children are instinctively more disciplined than adults whenever a new device enters the household, and so need no rules at all.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The passage never generalizes about children's discipline or says they need no rules; it records only that one grandfather was distracted, and later ledgers name 'Dad included' without ranking the generations.

options.text: inviting adult readers to see themselves as possible subjects of the rule, unsettling the pledge's assumption that only children need protecting.
options.label: correct
options.why: The audience consists of adults who received a card framed around children; the detail, reinforced by 'All of us' and 'to keep herself and her husband inside as much as anyone,' turns the rule toward the adults reading the essay.

options.text: establishing the grandmother as a careful keeper of household records whose ledger entries the reader can trust as evidence.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The ledger's precision does build credibility, but that is the work of the price and the dated entries, not of the detail about who was 'the trouble,' which speaks to the audience's assumptions about blame.

options.text: confirming the library's premise that the supper table must be reclaimed on behalf of the young from the adults who neglect it.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer explicitly resists the card's wording and later tells readers to cross out 'Give your children back the table'; the rule is for 'all of us,' not a reclamation on children's behalf.

items.stem: The writer's concession in paragraph 5 that "the ledgers do not record a single happy supper" primarily qualifies the argument by

options.text: narrowing what the shared hour is claimed to have produced from conversation to mere presence, which the writer then argues was itself worth keeping.
options.label: correct
options.why: The paragraph shifts the claim from 'produced conversation' to 'produced attendance,' then rebuts with 'attendance, it turns out, is not nothing' and the mother's detailed memory of the sullen suppers.

options.text: admitting that the household rule failed in practice and therefore suggesting that modern families should enforce it less rigidly, perhaps on weekends only.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer does not treat the rule as a failure or call for loosening it; she goes on to sign the card and urge readers to keep the hour 'every night.'

options.text: introducing nostalgia as the chief reason readers should sign the pledge, since remembered suppers, however idealized, matter more than the real ones did.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Nostalgia is named as a temptation the evidence corrects ('Nostalgia would have me believe'), not as a motive the writer endorses for signing.

options.text: setting aside the documentary record in favor of the writer's own childhood memories, which she presents as more reliable than ledgers or letters.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: The writer relies on the ledgers and letters throughout the concession and cites her mother's memory as additional support, not her own memories as a replacement for the record.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the function of paragraph 4 in the passage as a whole?

options.text: It defines two key terms in order to clarify the library's wording, which the writer finds ambiguous rather than mistaken and hopes the library will reword.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: The definitions serve the whole argument about rituals, and the writer finds the wording mistaken, not ambiguous, as her instruction to readers to cross it out shows.

options.text: It provides the conceptual distinction that reinterprets the family examples in paragraphs 2 and 3 and sets up the closing instruction about the pledge card.
options.label: correct
options.why: The curfew-ritual definition and the whistle-versus-warrant analogy explain why 'All of us' and 'Dad included' mattered, and they ground the final advice to cross out the card's line about children.

options.text: It shifts the evidence from family history to the economic life of the town, broadening the base of support for the writer's argument.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The mill whistle appears as an analogy for how the rule should feel, not as new evidence about the town's economy; the paragraph's work is conceptual, not evidentiary.

options.text: It anticipates and refutes the objection about sullen, silent suppers that the writer raises in the paragraph that follows, defusing it before it appears.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Paragraph 4 says nothing about the quality of the suppers; the concession is raised and answered within paragraph 5 itself.

items.stem: Paragraph 3 is developed primarily through

options.text: a chain of causes and effects, which shows that each new device forced the household to make the previous rule stricter than before.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The paragraph presents the rules as the same response each time, not as an escalating sequence in which one device caused a stricter rule for the next.

options.text: a problem-and-solution structure, which proposes unplugging devices as the remedy for the family quarrels each machine provoked at the supper table in turn.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: No quarrels are described in paragraph 3, and the writer stresses that the machines were not removed but scheduled ('it told the stranger when to call').

options.text: a contrast between generations, which exposes the grandmother's leniency toward the radio against the mother's far greater severity toward the television nearly thirty years later.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Both women wrote nearly identical rules ('All of us'; 'no exceptions, Dad included'); the paragraph stresses continuity, not a difference in strictness.

options.text: a chronological series of parallel examples, which establishes that the household's response to each new device was a repeated pattern rather than a single quirk.
options.label: correct
options.why: The paragraph lists 1954 and 1967 in parallel sentences after announcing 'The pattern repeated itself,' and concludes with 'each time the household did the same thing.'

items.stem: The two short sentences that close the passage, "The machine has changed. The fence has not," are most effective in conveying

options.text: a settled conclusion that distills the three-generation narrative into one principle, their brevity lending the writer's stance an air of certainty.
options.label: correct
options.why: After long sentences of instruction and narrative, the clipped pair reduces the radio, telephone, television and phone to 'the machine' and the recurring rule to 'the fence,' and the terse rhythm reads as assured finality.

options.text: a new counterargument about whether a rule from 1938 can still apply to devices that fit in a pocket.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The sentences answer, rather than raise, the question of applicability; the writer has already extended the rule to phones ('phone in the drawer') in the preceding sentence.

options.text: a resigned acknowledgment that new technology will keep arriving no matter what households decide to do about it.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The sentences are not resigned; the stress falls on the unchanged fence, which the writer treats as a dependable and chosen response, not on technology's inevitability.

options.text: a late reservation that the household rule, described as a fence, may now confine the family more than it protects them.
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: The word 'fence' has been established since paragraph 2 as a shared boundary built 'to keep herself and her husband inside'; nothing in the ending reverses that positive sense.

items.stem: The details in paragraph 1 suggest that the passage is most directly a response to which of the following situations?

options.text: A local institution has circulated a pledge whose practice the writer supports but whose wording she believes misplaces responsibility.
options.label: correct
options.why: Sentence 3 names the exact unease: she agrees with the proposal and distrusts its wording, and sentences 4 and 5 question who took the table from the children.

options.text: A local institution has asked households to give up their devices entirely, a demand the writer considers unrealistic for modern families.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The card asks only for screens down at supper (sentence 2); nothing in the passage indicates a demand to abandon devices, and the writer later praises keeping machines (sentence 16).

options.text: A reader of the magazine has argued publicly that the writer's own family history offers no guidance for households today.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: No challenge from a reader appears; the occasion is the arrival of the pledge card in the library's envelope (sentence 1).

options.text: A library newsletter has reported that children in the town are spending more hours on screens than their parents did at the same age.
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: The newsletter is mentioned only as the envelope's other contents (sentence 1); no report or comparison of children's screen hours is given anywhere in the passage.

items.stem: Taken together, paragraphs 3 and 6 best convey which of the following as the writer's stance toward new household machines?

options.text: They are intrusions that a careful household should keep out of the home as long as it reasonably can.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Sentence 15 states the household did not bar the stranger, and sentence 16 notes each machine stayed; the writer never recommends keeping machines out.

options.text: They are welcome once the household, adults included, decides when they may and may not have its attention.
options.label: correct
options.why: Sentences 15 through 17 describe telling the stranger when to call and marking off one hour, and sentence 30 directs the adult reader to put the phone in the drawer for that hour.

options.text: They are tolerable for adults, who can regulate themselves, but harmful to children until they learn restraint.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The passage repeatedly locates the problem with adults (sentences 9, 14, 29, 30), not with children who must learn restraint.

options.text: They are each less disruptive than the one before, so households now have little reason to regulate them.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The writer presents the pattern as recurring and still necessary (sentences 12, 32, 33); she never ranks machines by disruptiveness or suggests regulation is now unneeded.

items.stem: In paragraph 2, the writer's inclusion of the radio's price, "thirty-one dollars and forty cents," as recorded in the ledger primarily functions to

options.text: establish that the family's hardship, not the grandfather's habits, explains why the radio was restricted at meals
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The passage attributes the rule to the grandfather's behavior (sentence 9), not to cost; the price is never linked to the reason for the restriction.

options.text: lend documentary precision to a family story that might otherwise seem like fond invention
options.label: correct
options.why: Sentence 6 ties the exact figure to a ledger kept in the grandmother's hand, and sentences 7 and 8 continue to cite the ledger as a record, grounding the anecdote in a written source.

options.text: signal that the writer has verified the ledger's figures against other historical records of the period
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The writer cites only the household ledger (sentence 6); no outside verification or comparison with other records is mentioned.

options.text: suggest that the family valued the radio too highly to have ever considered removing it from the house
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The price is offered as a ledger detail, not as an explanation of attachment; the decision to keep rather than bar machines is argued separately in sentence 15.

items.stem: Which of the following sentences from the passage most fully states the writer's central claim?

options.text: "The pattern repeated itself with a regularity that would be comic if it were not so instructive."
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Sentence 12 introduces the enumeration in paragraph 3 and asserts repetition, but it says nothing about the curfew-versus-ritual distinction that the essay builds toward.

options.text: "There is a difference, I think, between a curfew and a ritual, and the difference matters more than the hour chosen."
options.label: correct
options.why: Sentence 18 names the distinction that reinterprets the anecdotes of paragraphs 2 and 3, anchors the concession in paragraph 5, and drives the instruction to cross out the second line in paragraph 6.

options.text: "Nostalgia would have me believe that the quiet hour produced conversation; the evidence suggests only that it produced attendance."
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Sentence 25 is the narrowing move within the concession; it qualifies a supporting point rather than stating the governing argument about shared ritual.

options.text: "My grandmother knew this in 1938 with a radio she could barely afford."
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Sentence 31 is a closing gesture that refers back to the claim with the pronoun 'this'; it depends on earlier sentences and does not itself state the claim.

items.stem: The 1967 ledger entry quoted in paragraph 3, "Set off at supper, no exceptions, Dad included," most directly serves as evidence for the claim that

options.text: the household's rules grew stricter with each new machine as the children became teenagers
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Nothing indicates escalating strictness; the passage stresses that the household did 'the same thing' each time (sentence 15).

options.text: the grandmother's rule had failed by the next generation and had to be written down again from scratch
options.label: reversal
options.why: Sentence 12 frames the new entry as the pattern repeating, a continuity rather than a failure; the writer treats the repetition as instructive, not as a collapse.

options.text: the family's supper rule, across generations, bound the adults of the household as explicitly as it bound the young
options.label: correct
options.why: The quoted phrase 'Dad included' echoes sentence 11, where the grandmother built the fence to keep herself and her husband inside, showing the rule's application to adults persisted into 1967.

options.text: television proved more tempting to the family than the radio or telephone had been
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The passage does not compare the pull of the machines; the entry names the father, paralleling the radio story (sentence 9), rather than ranking devices.

items.stem: The two questions that close paragraph 1, "Give the children back the table? Who, exactly, had taken it from them?", prepare the reader for the rest of the passage primarily by

options.text: announcing that the writer will refuse the pledge and explain her refusal through family history
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer signs the card (sentence 28); her unease is with the wording, not the proposal (sentence 3).

options.text: posing a question of responsibility that the family narrative then answers by pointing to the adults
options.label: correct
options.why: The question of who took the table is answered in sentence 9 (the grandfather was the trouble), sentence 14 ('Dad included'), and sentence 29 ('Do not give the children back the table').

options.text: establishing a playful tone that the writer sustains through the historical paragraphs and the closing appeal
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The tone shifts to wry narration, then candid concession, then assured exhortation (sentences 12, 23, 28); the questions voice unease, not sustained play.

options.text: introducing the distinction between curfew and ritual that paragraph 4 will define in detail
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: The questions concern who is responsible for leaving the table; the curfew-versus-ritual distinction is a separate conceptual move introduced only in sentence 18.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the relationship between paragraph 2 and paragraph 3?

options.text: Paragraph 2 presents a single founding example, and paragraph 3 shows that the household's response recurred with each later machine.
options.label: correct
options.why: Sentence 12 opens paragraph 3 with 'The pattern repeated itself,' and sentences 13 through 16 enumerate the telephone and television following the same scheduling response established in sentences 8 through 11.

options.text: Paragraph 2 describes a rule that worked, and paragraph 3 explains why later generations found it impossible to maintain.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Paragraph 3 shows the rule being renewed, not abandoned; the 1967 ledger entry repeats the grandmother's rule (sentence 14).

options.text: Paragraph 2 relies on family memory, and paragraph 3 corrects that memory with written records from the ledgers.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Both paragraphs draw on ledgers and memory alike (sentences 6, 8, 9, 13, 14); paragraph 3 does not correct paragraph 2.

options.text: Paragraph 2 narrates the grandmother's rule, and paragraph 3 defines the terms that make the rule a ritual rather than a curfew.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The definitions of curfew and ritual belong to paragraph 4 (sentences 18 through 20); paragraph 3 extends the narrative pattern rather than defining terms.

items.stem: In paragraph 5, the sentence "But attendance, it turns out, is not nothing" is most logically effective because it

options.text: withdraws the preceding concession and reasserts that the quiet hour did in fact produce conversation
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer never retracts the admission; sentence 25 grants that the hour produced only attendance, and sentence 27 continues to describe the suppers as sullen.

options.text: accepts the narrowed claim of the previous sentence and then asserts that the narrowed claim still carries weight
options.label: correct
options.why: Sentence 25 reduces the hour's benefit to attendance; sentence 26 accepts that reduction with 'But' and 'not nothing,' and sentence 27 supplies the memory evidence that attendance is what endured.

options.text: introduces new ledger evidence that contradicts the letters describing sullen, silent meals
options.label: unsupported
options.why: No new ledger evidence appears; sentence 27 offers the mother's memory, which confirms rather than contradicts that the suppers were sullen.

options.text: shifts the argument from the family's history to the reader's household before the final paragraph begins
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The turn to the reader occurs in sentence 28 with 'I would urge you'; sentence 26 remains within the evaluation of the family's recorded suppers.

items.stem: In paragraph 6, the structure of the sentence "Sit down at it yourself, phone in the drawer, and let them see you, every night, until the hour belongs to all of you and nobody remembers whom it was meant to protect" emphasizes the relationship between ideas by

options.text: opening with a dependent clause that states the goal, so that the commands which follow appear as mere suggestions
options.label: convention_error
options.why: The sentence begins with imperatives ('Sit down,' 'let them see you'), not with a dependent clause; the 'until' clause is placed last.

options.text: placing a series of imperatives first and the "until" clause last, so that the actions lead toward an end point in which the rule's original target is forgotten
options.label: correct
options.why: The commands come first, with the interrupting phrases 'phone in the drawer' and 'every night,' and the final subordinate clause names the outcome: shared ownership and no memory of whom it protected, which answers paragraph 1's question.

options.text: balancing two independent clauses of equal weight, so that the parent's action and the child's observation appear as separate obligations
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The clauses are coordinated imperatives aimed at the same adult reader, and the child's role is to see the adult; nothing presents the child as bearing an obligation.

options.text: repeating the word "you" at the start of each clause, so that the reader is singled out as the person the pledge was designed to protect
options.label: reversal
options.why: 'You' is not clause-initial, and the sentence ends by saying nobody remembers whom the rule protected; the reader is addressed as the adult who must comply, not as the protected party.

items.stem: In paragraph 2, the colon in the sentence "By the following Sunday a second entry appears, not a sum but a sentence: 'No set from six to seven. All of us.'" is most effective because it

options.text: holds back the ledger's words until the contrast between a sum and a sentence has been set up, giving the handwritten rule the weight of a quoted document
options.label: correct
options.why: The clause before the colon builds expectation by noting the entry is 'not a sum but a sentence,' and the colon then presents the rule itself, which the essay later treats as its key text (sentence 22, 'All of us').

options.text: separates the writer's own commentary on the rule from the grandmother's words so that readers can judge the rule without the writer's interpretation
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The material before the colon is description of the ledger, not commentary on the rule; interpretation comes afterward in sentences 10 and 11, not before.

options.text: signals that the ledger entry was written hastily, in the moment of frustration with the grandfather's listening
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Nothing about the punctuation or the surrounding text suggests haste; the entry appears five days after the purchase (sentences 7 and 8), and the grandfather's behavior is explained only in sentence 9.

options.text: joins two independent statements about the purchase so that the Tuesday entry and the Sunday entry read as a single financial record
options.label: convention_error
options.why: The colon introduces a quotation, not a second independent clause, and the Sunday entry is explicitly 'not a sum,' distinguishing it from the financial record of the purchase.

blueprint.purpose: To persuade the city council to require fully shielded fixtures in the streetlight replacement ordinance
blueprint.audience: Larkhaven City Council members and residents attending a public hearing
blueprint.claim: Unshielded streetlights are erasing Larkhaven's night sky, and shielded fixtures could restore it at no added cost.
blueprint.theme: amateur astronomy and the dark-sky movement

planned_flaws.flaw: vague thesis that neither takes a position nor previews the argument
introduction never connects the speaker to the agenda item under discussion
anecdote left without commentary tying it to the claim
statistic from another town not explained or linked to reasoning
wordy, redundant sentence with a doubled subject
casual conclusion that makes no request and fits neither the formal occasion nor the persuasive purpose

provenance.note: Fictional testimony draft for a Larkhaven council hearing

g-lw04.title: Testimony on Ordinance 14-B
paragraphs: Good evening, members of the Larkhaven City Council.
My name is Odile Strand, and I have lived on Quarry Hill Road for twenty-two years.
Tonight I want to talk about lights.
Every second Saturday, the Larkhaven Stargazers Club sets up telescopes in the gravel lot behind the public library.
Ten years ago, we could show visitors the faint smudge of the Andromeda galaxy without much trouble.
Since the city installed the new white LED globes along Cutler Avenue, that smudge has disappeared from our lot entirely.
Last spring a nine-year-old girl looked through my eyepiece, saw only a gray haze, and asked whether the telescope was broken.
The problem is not that the lights are on but where they point.
The Cutler Avenue fixtures are uncovered globes that throw about a third of their light sideways and upward, where it lights nothing but the sky.
The town of Fenwick Ridge, forty miles north, replaced its globes with fully shielded fixtures and reported that its electricity bill for street lighting dropped by 18 percent.
Shielded fixtures, which aim light downward toward the street, they cost about the same as the globes the city currently uses and they also last just as long as the globes do.
Anyway, that is basically all I have got, so thanks for listening to me ramble.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 12 with a conclusion that suits a formal hearing, asks the council for a specific action on the ordinance, and returns to an image from earlier in the testimony. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Honestly, those Cutler Avenue globes are a total eyesore, and you folks should rip every one of them out tomorrow, no matter what anyone else says.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Too casual and combative for council testimony, and it ignores the earlier image.

options.text: Astronomy has given me decades of joy, and I hope that more residents of Larkhaven will join our club on Saturdays and discover it for themselves.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Promotes the club rather than requesting any action on the ordinance.

options.text: Thank you for your time this evening, and I would be happy to answer any questions the council may have for me about my remarks.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Appropriately formal, but makes no request and recalls nothing from the testimony.

options.text: I urge you to require shielded fixtures in Ordinance 14-B, so that the next child at our eyepiece sees a galaxy instead of a haze.
options.label: correct
options.why: Formal, makes a specific request about the ordinance, and echoes the girl's gray haze from sentence 7.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 2 that tells the council why she is speaking by linking her introduction to the agenda item under discussion. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Quarry Hill Road is a quiet street, and in summer my neighbors often sit outside on their porches after dinner.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Adds neighborhood detail but never mentions the ordinance or why she is testifying.

options.text: I am here as a member of the Larkhaven Stargazers Club to speak on Ordinance 14-B, the streetlight replacement plan.
options.label: correct
options.why: Names her role and the specific agenda item, so the introduction leads into the testimony.

options.text: Before I retired, I worked as a pharmacist at a small drugstore on the east side of town for many years.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Gives personal background that has nothing to do with lighting or the agenda item.

options.text: Many cities around the world are now debating how much artificial light their residents actually need at night.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Talks about a global debate instead of the specific local agenda item.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 3 into a thesis that takes a position needing proof and previews both the problem and the solution she discusses later. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Light pollution has become a growing problem facing many towns and cities across the country and around the world in recent decades.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: A general observation that previews none of the draft's specific argument.

options.text: Tonight I want to share my lifelong love of astronomy, a hobby I have enjoyed ever since I was a child.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Personal and not arguable; it previews neither the lighting problem nor the solution.

options.text: I will ask the council to ban all outdoor lighting in Larkhaven after midnight in order to protect the sky.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Proposes a ban that the draft never argues for; the draft calls for shielding, not darkness.

options.text: I will argue that unshielded streetlights are erasing our night sky and that shielded fixtures could restore it at no added cost.
options.label: correct
options.why: Takes an arguable position and previews both the problem (paragraph 2) and the solution (paragraph 3).

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 7 that explains how the girl's experience supports her claim that the new lighting has hidden the night sky. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The telescope was working fine; what she saw was the glow of Cutler Avenue covering a sky our children once shared.
options.label: correct
options.why: Turns the anecdote into evidence by blaming the haze on the streetlights, which supports the claim.

options.text: Telescopes like mine can cost several hundred dollars, so her worry that it was broken was a perfectly fair one to raise.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Comments on what the equipment costs instead of connecting the haze to the lighting.

options.text: I explained to her that the Andromeda galaxy, our nearest large neighbor, is roughly two and a half million light-years from Earth.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Adds a fact about astronomy but does not explain how the anecdote supports the claim about the lights.

options.text: She was easily the most curious child who has visited our club at any point in the last decade.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Praises the girl with no support and has no link to the argument about lighting.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 10 that explains how the Fenwick Ridge example supports her argument, building on the point in sentence 9 about wasted light. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: This proves that every city and town in the state would save exactly 18 percent right away by switching to shielded fixtures.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Overgeneralizes one town's result instead of explaining it.

options.text: Because shielded fixtures stop sending light into the sky, a town pays only for light that actually reaches its streets.
options.label: correct
options.why: Uses the wasted light from sentence 9 to explain why shielding reduced Fenwick Ridge's bill.

options.text: Fenwick Ridge is also known for its fall apple festival, which draws visitors from all across the region.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: An irrelevant detail about the town that explains nothing about the evidence.

options.text: Fenwick Ridge, like Larkhaven, is full of residents who care deeply about their community and its long-term future.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Claims the towns are alike but does not connect the savings to shielding or wasted light.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 11 so that it is concise and grammatically correct while keeping both of its claims about cost and durability. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Shielded fixtures, which aim light downward toward the street, cost about the same as the city's current globes and last just as long.
options.label: correct
options.why: Drops the doubled subject and repeated words but keeps both claims.

options.text: Shielded fixtures, which aim light downward toward the street, they cost about the same as the city's globes and last as long.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: Keeps the extra subject pronoun 'they,' which is ungrammatical.

options.text: Shielded fixtures, which aim light down toward the street below, are similar in cost to the globes the city uses now and are also similar in how long they last.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Grammatically correct but still wordy and repetitive.

options.text: Shielded fixtures, which aim light downward toward the street, cost somewhat more than the city's current globes but last much longer.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Changes both claims and weakens the writer's point that switching costs nothing extra.

items.stem: Some council members have said they worry that dimmer streets would be less safe. The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 9 that addresses this concern while keeping the focus on where the light points. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Because shielded fixtures send that wasted light down to the pavement, Cutler Avenue would stay just as bright where walkers and drivers need it.
options.label: correct
options.why: It answers the safety worry directly and ties it to sentence 9's point about misdirected light.

options.text: Honestly, anyone who thinks a dark sky makes streets dangerous has probably never stood in our library lot after sunset.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Dismisses the council's concern instead of answering it, which would alienate the audience she needs to persuade.

options.text: Shielded fixtures would cut crime on Cutler Avenue by half, making it the safest street in all of Larkhaven within a year.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Makes a sweeping claim about crime with no evidence anywhere in the testimony.

options.text: Many members of our club also enjoy photographing the moon, which looks clearer in a dark sky than under the white globes.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Moves to a hobby detail and never takes up the safety concern.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 6 that gives evidence showing the new Cutler Avenue globes, and not some other cause, are what hid the galaxy. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Last October, when an outage darkened Cutler Avenue for one night, our members found Andromeda from the same lot within minutes.
options.label: correct
options.why: With only the globes removed, the galaxy came back, which isolates the lights as the cause.

options.text: Andromeda is about two and a half million light-years away, which makes it one of the most distant objects visible to the eye.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: A general astronomy fact about the galaxy; it says nothing about what caused the loss.

options.text: Our club has grown from six members to more than forty, and most of our new members are families from the east side of town.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Club details stay on the topic but give no evidence about what is causing the problem.

options.text: Skies across the whole region have grown brighter for decades as towns and highways have expanded in every direction.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Points to regional growth as a cause, which weakens the claim that the Cutler globes are responsible.

items.stem: The writer wants to begin sentence 10 with a transition showing that, after describing the problem in sentence 9, she is now offering proof that it can be solved. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Fortunately, this waste can be fixed:
options.label: correct
options.why: It marks a shift from problem to solution and introduces Fenwick Ridge as proof.

options.text: As a result of this waste,
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Suggests the sideways light caused Fenwick Ridge's savings, which makes no sense.

options.text: Even so, despite this waste,
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Signals contrast or concession, but sentence 10 builds on the point instead of pushing against it.

options.text: In other words, put simply,
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Signals a restatement, but sentence 10 brings in new evidence from another town.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 8 so that the two parts of the "not ... but" construction are grammatically parallel. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The problem is not that the lights are on but that they point the wrong way.
options.label: correct
options.why: Both halves are "that" clauses, so the construction is parallel and the meaning is clear.

options.text: The problem is not that the lights are on but their pointing the wrong way.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: Pairs a "that" clause with a gerund phrase, so the halves are still not parallel.

options.text: The problem is not that the lights are on, but, where they point.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: Adds commas that don't belong and still leaves the halves unparallel.

options.text: The problem is not the lights being on but that they are pointed wrongly.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Changes the wording, but it now pairs a noun phrase with a clause and is still not parallel.

blueprint.purpose: To persuade local readers to donate during the community radio station's fortieth-anniversary pledge drive
blueprint.audience: General readers of a small-town weekly newspaper, many of them longtime residents and listeners
blueprint.claim: Harrow Bend should support Riverbend Community Radio because it serves the town in ways streaming services cannot.
blueprint.theme: community radio in the streaming age

planned_flaws.flaw: Vague, generic opening
Overstated claim that every person was listening
Absolute dismissal of algorithms
Claim about ordinary people lacks an example
Mocking, flippant tone undercuts appeal
Comma splice
Flat conclusion that does not call readers to act

g-lw32.title: Forty Years on 89.7
paragraphs: Radio is a thing that many people have listened to over the years.
This Saturday, Riverbend Community Radio turns forty, and its volunteers will spend the weekend asking listeners for enough money to replace a transmitter older than most of its DJs.
I think the town should give generously, because the little station on Kettle Street does something no streaming app can do.
Streaming services know what I like, but they do not know where I live.
When the Oxbow River flooded in March, it was 89.7 FM that told us which roads were closed and which church basement had dry cots.
Volunteer Hal Pruitt stayed on the air for nineteen hours, reading messages from neighbors looking for lost dogs and elderly parents.
Every single person in Harrow Bend was listening that night.
No algorithm will ever do anything useful for a small town.
The station is also a kind of town square.
On Tuesday nights, high school students host a show about their marching band's season, and on Sunday mornings retired farmers argue about rainfall totals.
The station's budget is pathetic, and frankly the fact that it survives at all is kind of a joke.
Yet it does survive, because ordinary people keep it going.
The pledge drive runs from 6 a.m. Saturday until midnight Sunday, a donation of 25 dollars keeps the station on the air for about an hour.
So, that's my opinion on radio.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 14 with a closing sentence that urges readers to donate and returns to the contrast introduced in sentence 4. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Your playlist will keep guessing what you like; this weekend, pledge to the one station that knows where you live.
options.label: correct
options.why: Calls readers to pledge and echoes the like/live contrast from sentence 4.

options.text: Radio has changed a great deal in forty years, and it will surely keep changing in the decades ahead.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Generic reflection on radio; no call to donate and no link to sentence 4.

options.text: Streaming apps offer millions of songs, so perhaps local radio like 89.7 has simply had its day and should quietly sign off.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Undercuts the column's argument by suggesting the station should close instead of urging support.

options.text: Hal Pruitt's nineteen hours on the air during the flood deserve a bronze plaque in the station's front lobby.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Focuses on one volunteer rather than urging donations or returning to the streaming contrast.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 7 so that it no longer overstates the station's audience but still suggests how widely the broadcast was heard. Which revision best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Some people in Harrow Bend prefer podcasts to the radio on most ordinary weeknights after dinner.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Shifts to listening habits generally, not the flood-night audience.

options.text: Judging by the calls the station logged, hundreds of households in Harrow Bend were listening that night.
options.label: correct
options.why: Replaces the absolute claim with a qualified, evidence-based estimate that still shows wide reach.

options.text: Absolutely everyone in Harrow Bend, without a single exception, had the station on all through that night.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Intensifies the overstatement rather than qualifying it.

options.text: A few people in Harrow Bend may have had their radios turned on that night.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Qualifies the claim but abandons the sense of wide reach the writer wants.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 8 to acknowledge what streaming services do well while maintaining the paragraph's point about local service. Which revision best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Algorithms are useless, and anyone who relies on them is foolishly ignoring what really matters in life and in this town.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Remains absolute and adds a dismissive jab; acknowledges nothing.

options.text: An algorithm may be good at finding me a new song, but no algorithm found my neighbor a dry cot.
options.label: correct
options.why: Concedes a real strength of streaming, then reasserts the station's local value using the flood detail.

options.text: Many streaming companies were founded in the past two decades by large technology firms based in distant coastal cities.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Offers off-topic background instead of a concession tied to local service.

options.text: Algorithms are better than radio in nearly every way, including during floods, storms, and other local emergencies like the one in March.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Concedes so much it contradicts the paragraph's point, even about the March flood.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 12 that gives a specific example supporting the claim that ordinary people keep the station going. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Ordinary people are truly the backbone of the station, and without their steady help it simply could not survive.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Restates the claim without any specific example.

options.text: Many community stations across the country face similar money troubles in the streaming era, from Maine to rural Oregon.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Generalizes nationally; gives no example of local people keeping this station alive.

options.text: Last winter, when the roof leaked, a local roofer patched it for free and the bakery next door paid for shingles.
options.label: correct
options.why: Concrete example of ordinary residents sustaining the station.

options.text: The transmitter that needs replacing was installed when the station first went on the air forty years ago this spring.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Repeats the transmitter detail and does not show people sustaining the station.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 11 so that it conveys a sincere, admiring tone suited to readers being asked to donate. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The station's budget is a total disaster, and honestly it's a miracle the thing hasn't collapsed already.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Still flippant and disparaging, discouraging donors.

options.text: The station runs on a budget smaller than the high school band's, which makes its survival nothing short of remarkable.
options.label: correct
options.why: Respectful and admiring; sets up 'Yet it does survive' and keeps the local detail.

options.text: The station is very well funded by state grants and has never had much trouble paying its bills on time.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Contradicts the need for the pledge drive, invents funding, and makes sentence 12 illogical.

options.text: Fiscal resources allocated to the station remain suboptimal relative to its operational requirements and projected capital expenditure needs.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Stiff bureaucratic jargon, not sincere or warm for newspaper readers.

items.stem: The writer wants to correct the punctuation error in sentence 13. Which revision of the portion "midnight Sunday, a donation" correctly joins the two independent clauses?

options.text: midnight Sunday, because a donation
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Grammatical, but falsely claims the schedule exists because of the donation rate.

options.text: midnight Sunday a donation
options.label: convention_error
options.why: Creates a run-on sentence with no punctuation between clauses.

options.text: midnight Sunday, and, a donation
options.label: convention_error
options.why: The comma after 'and' is incorrect and interrupts the clause.

options.text: midnight Sunday; a donation
options.label: correct
options.why: A semicolon correctly joins two independent clauses, fixing the comma splice.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 2 that appeals to longtime residents by calling up their own memories of the station. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Many of us first heard 89.7 as children, crackling through the kitchen radio on snow-day mornings.
options.label: correct
options.why: It draws on a shared, concrete memory that longtime local listeners are likely to have, connecting with their values right before the appeal for money.

options.text: Older listeners may not realize how outdated broadcast radio looks to most people today.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: It talks down to the longtime residents the writer hopes will donate and calls the station outdated, which works against the appeal.

options.text: Surveys show that nine out of ten residents rank the station as their favorite local institution.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: It brings in a survey nobody can check instead of calling up personal memories, so it does not meet the stated goal.

options.text: Community radio stations across the country have been struggling to pay for equipment lately.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: It moves to a national trend and says nothing about local listeners' own memories of 89.7.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 3 into a thesis that makes a claim needing proof and previews both body paragraphs (the flood coverage and the station as a town square). Which revision best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The town should give generously, because the station on Kettle Street keeps us informed in a crisis and gives neighbors a place to hear one another.
options.label: correct
options.why: It makes an arguable claim and names both reasons, emergency information and the town-square role, in the same order as paragraphs 2 and 3.

options.text: Riverbend Community Radio has broadcast from Kettle Street for forty years, through floods, band seasons, and long arguments about rain.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: It is a statement of fact that needs no proof, so it does not work as a thesis even though it mentions the topics.

options.text: The town should give generously, because the station on Kettle Street was the only reliable source of news during the March flood.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: It previews only the flood paragraph and leaves out the town-square paragraph.

options.text: The town should give generously to every local institution, because small-town media of all kinds are disappearing faster than ever.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: It widens the claim beyond the station and does not preview either body paragraph.

items.stem: The writer wants to add commentary after sentence 6 that explains how Hal Pruitt's broadcast supports the claim in sentence 4. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: No playlist could have found a lost dog on Mill Road, because only a voice from Harrow Bend knew which neighbors were asking.
options.label: correct
options.why: It ties the evidence (the local messages Pruitt read) to the claim that streaming services do not know where listeners live.

options.text: Pruitt kept reading message after message for nineteen hours, pausing only for coffee and the weather report.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: It adds more detail about the evidence but never explains how that evidence supports sentence 4.

g-lw06.title: What the Shoreline Taught Us: A Report on Merrow Point's Retreating Coast
paragraphs: The ocean has always been a powerful force in human history.
This fall, our environmental science class spent nine weeks measuring the bluffs along Gannet Road.
We used survey stakes, old aerial photographs from the town library, and interviews with eleven residents.
What we found out and discovered in the end was that the bluff edge has moved back an average of about two feet every single year since 1990.
The town's first answer to erosion was the concrete seawall built below Pell Street in 1998.
The wall protected the houses directly behind it for many years.
Anyone who still thinks walls are the answer simply has not looked at the beach.
Waves bouncing off the concrete have scoured away the sand in front of it, and the beach at Pell Street has nearly vanished.
Dune restoration is a better way to protect the coast.
Last spring, volunteers planted beach grass and set sand fences along the north end of Little Cove.
Our stake measurements there showed that the bluff lost less than four inches this year, compared with two feet near the seawall.
The town has also moved the Gannet Road pump station 200 feet inland, and the lifeguard tower now sits on movable skids.
Moving buildings is expensive.
Rebuilding them after a storm costs more.
Our class recommends that the council fund more dune planting and begin planning which structures should move first.

items.stem: Many council members own shorefront homes and supported the seawall. The writer wants to revise sentence 7 so it acknowledges their view respectfully while still pointing to the wall's drawback. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The wall made sense when it was built, but its effect on the beach in front of it deserves a closer look.
options.label: correct

options.text: Some people like walls and some people like dunes, and everyone is entitled to an opinion about how the town should handle its coast.
options.label: wrong_function

options.text: Supporters of the wall were frankly shortsighted, though they probably meant well when they voted to pour concrete below Pell Street.
options.label: wrong_tone

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 9 that offers evidence supporting the claim that dune restoration specifically protects the coast. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.label: too_narrow

options.text: At the town's older restored dune near Hollis Beach, our stakes showed almost no bluff loss over three years of storms.

options.text: Erosion is a problem that affects shorelines on every continent and costs governments large sums each year in repairs to roads and harbors.

options.label: correct

g-lw22.title: Eight Bars at the Grange Hall
paragraphs: Last Thursday I sat in the back row of the Fenwick Grange Hall while the Marrow Creek Community Orchestra rehearsed for its spring concert.
Orchestras are interesting and say a lot about people.
Forty-one players showed up, from a fourteen-year-old violist to a retired mail carrier who has played second trombone for thirty years.
Conductor Abel Ostrander stopped the group six times in the first piece, each time over the same eight bars.
The flutes were rushing, the cellos were dragging, and nobody could hear the oboe.
Ostrander did not single anyone out; instead, he asked every section except the oboe to play the passage half as loud.
By the fourth try, the oboe melody floated clearly over the whole ensemble.
Every musician in an orchestra always cares more about the group than about his or her own part.
During the break, the cellists told me their section meets on Sunday afternoons to work through tricky passages together.
Players share music stands, and the woodwinds carry spare reeds for anyone who forgets theirs.
The orchestra holds no auditions, anyone who can read music is welcome.
Our town council, which spent last winter arguing over a parking lot could learn something from them.
Anyway, that is what I saw at the rehearsal.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 13 with a conclusion that urges readers to attend the May 10 concert and also ties back to the column's point about cooperation. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Honestly, anyone who skips this concert is missing out, and frankly they should be embarrassed to admit they had better things to do that night.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Scolding tone suits neither the audience nor the column, and it omits cooperation.

options.text: Hear it yourself on May 10 at the Grange Hall, and listen for the oboe: it rises only because everyone else chose to play softer.
options.label: correct
options.why: Invites readers to the concert and recalls the rehearsal moment that shows cooperation.

options.text: The concert is on May 10 at the Grange Hall, tickets cost eight dollars at the door, and there will be lemonade and cookies during intermission.
options.label: partially_right

options.text: In the end, cooperation is what holds an orchestra together, just as it holds together a family, a team, or any other group of people.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Restates the theme but never urges readers to attend the concert.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 2 into a thesis that makes a claim requiring proof and previews both the rehearsal scene and the later comparison to the town council. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The orchestra has rehearsed in the Fenwick Grange Hall since 1987 and gives two free concerts there every spring and fall.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: A statement of fact that needs no proof and previews nothing.

options.text: I came to believe the orchestra's players listen carefully to one another, section by section, before any of them plays a note.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Covers the rehearsal but does not preview the comparison to the town council.

options.text: Watching them, I came to believe an orchestra works because its players listen before they play, a habit our leaders could borrow.
options.label: correct
options.why: Arguable claim about listening that previews both the rehearsal and the council comparison.

options.text: Music has brought people together in every culture and every century throughout human history, from ancient temples to modern stadiums.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Sweeping claim far beyond the column's local focus; no preview of the council point.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 8 so that it acknowledges that individual players still care about their own parts while keeping the column's point about cooperation. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Some musicians in this orchestra have played together for decades, carpool to rehearsals, and know one another's families, jobs, and hometowns well.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Shifts to a different topic and drops both the concession and the cooperation claim.

options.text: Most musicians care only about their own parts, and the group sound that results is mostly an accident nobody really plans for.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Contradicts the column's argument rather than qualifying it.

options.text: Players still want their own parts to sound good, of course, but the best of them will step back when the music needs it.
options.label: correct
options.why: Concedes individual pride and still affirms cooperation, removing the absolute claim.

options.text: Every single musician in every orchestra in the world cares far more about the group than about anything else, including their own playing.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Intensifies the overstatement instead of qualifying it.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 7 that explains how the rehearsal moment illustrates cooperation. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The oboist, a dental hygienist named Ruth Palko, has played with the group for nine years and teaches lessons on weekends.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Adds a detail but no commentary connecting the evidence to the claim.

options.text: This proves that the oboe is the most important instrument in any orchestra and that composers should always give it the melody.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Draws a conclusion the evidence does not support and misses the cooperation point.

options.text: After that, the orchestra moved on to rehearse a lively march, full of brass fanfares, that would close the spring concert.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Continues the narration rather than explaining the moment's significance.

options.text: The fix came not from one player trying harder but from everyone agreeing to make room for a single voice.
options.label: correct
options.why: Explains that the improvement resulted from the group yielding, linking the evidence to cooperation.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 12 so that readers of the weekly paper who sit on or support the town council will take the comparison as an invitation, not an insult. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Our town council, which worked hard last winter on a difficult parking lot decision, might find a useful habit in those Sunday cello sessions.
options.label: correct
options.why: It credits the council's effort and offers the orchestra's habit as a helpful model, so council supporters are not put on the defensive.

options.text: Our town council, which wasted all of last winter bickering over a parking lot, should be embarrassed by a group of amateur musicians.
options.label: wrong_tone

options.text: Our town council, which has argued over many issues besides parking for years now, has never once managed to agree on anything at all.
options.label: unsupported

options.text: Our town council, which meets on the second Tuesday of each month in the hall, also uses the Grange building for its public hearings.
options.label: wrong_function

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 3 that would appeal to newspaper readers who think orchestras are only for trained or wealthy people. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Most of them have day jobs, and several borrowed their instruments from the school band closet.
options.label: correct
options.why: It shows ordinary, low-cost membership, which speaks directly to readers who see orchestras as elite.

options.text: Several of them studied at conservatories before they settled in the area to raise families.
options.label: reversal
options.why: It confirms the elite image the writer is trying to correct.

options.text: The program includes two symphonies and an overture that is known for its very hard horn parts.
options.label: wrong_function

options.label: too_broad

items.stem: The writer wants to begin sentence 10 with a transition that signals it gives more examples of the same kind of cooperation described in sentence 9. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.label: correct
options.why: It marks sentence 10 as more examples of the shared effort in sentence 9.

options.text: On the other hand,
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: It signals a contrast, but sentence 10 builds on sentence 9 instead of opposing it.

options.why: Sentence 9 does not cause the sharing of stands and reeds, so a cause-and-effect link is false.

options.text: Despite these meetings,
options.label: reversal

items.stem: The writer wants to add an analogy after sentence 6 that helps general readers see why making room for others, as in this rehearsal, can make one voice heard. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: It was like a dinner table going quiet so the shy cousin at the end can finally finish her story.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 10 that explains how the details in sentences 9 and 10 support the column's claim that the orchestra works because its players look out for one another. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?
